title: Yemeni forces' retreat leaves Houthis in control of key area on coast of Red Sea waterway
excerpt:
Pro-government forces said troops were being moved to defend the interim capital, Aden (file photo)

Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia have said they are withdrawing from an area ove...
body_text:
Pro-government forces said troops were being moved to defend the interim capital, Aden (file photo)

Yemeni pro-government forces backed by Saudi Arabia have said they are withdrawing from an area overlooking the strategically important Bab al-Mandab Strait, leaving it under the control of the Iran-backed Houthi movement.

Yemen's military said it was redeploying troops from the key shipping gateway at the southern end of the Red Sea to defend its interim capital, Aden.

The shift ends a weeks-long offensive to try to secure the area near the waterway after the Houthis seized it in a surprise offensive in September, squeezing global oil exports and prompting thousands to flee.

Houthi-run media reported later on Sunday the group had taken control of the territory. Saudi Arabia has not commented.

Pro-government forces said they had "secured" the strait in early October as they sought to retake crucial ground from the Houthis, who said they had captured areas including Perim Island at the mouth of the strait and the strategic port city of Mokha a month prior.

Watch: Why is the Bab al-Mandab Strait so important?

But the Saudi-backed forces fighting on behalf of Yemen's internationally recognised government said on Sunday they were withdrawing to reinforce troops elsewhere, with the southern city of Aden a "priority".

The Southern Armed Forces' statement said troops were being withdrawn "from Dhubab Airport and the Bab al-Mandab area".

It said the decision had been made with the aim of "strengthening the front lines and addressing existing threats".

"This step is driven by the priority of securing the capital, Aden, and neighbouring governorates, reinforcing the front lines and addressing existing threats."

The Houthis said they posed no threat to international shipping passing through the waterway when they captured it, but that they would continue to target vessels from Saudi Arabia.

However, the seizure contributed to a surge in global oil prices because Saudi Arabia had been relying on the Red Sea for oil exports since the US and Israel's war with Iran effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz.

A UN Human Rights spokesperson, Ravina Shamdasani, urged all parties to protect civilians and civilian infrastructure.

She noted that since the escalation of fighting in August, more than 60% of documented civilian casualties were women and children.

The Houthis have repeatedly attacked the city of Aden in recent weeks, including an assault on 15 October that targeted the presidential palace, killing five and injuring 16.

Saudi Arabia responded with hundreds of air strikes, while the Houthis launched hundreds of drones and missiles at its cities and infrastructure.

The UN has estimated that nearly 330,000 people have been displaced in Yemen as the fighting has since escalated. Hundreds of people are reported to have been killed.

Why is the Bab al-Mandab Strait so important?

Yemeni military says it has 'secured' Red Sea waterway

Yemenis flee across Red Sea as Houthis and Saudi-backed forces escalate war

Yemen has been devastated by a civil war that began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the government from its capital, Sanaa.

The conflict escalated in 2015 after a Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.

title: Russia’s Andreeva defeats Ukraine’s Svitolina 7-5, 6-3 to win WTA Finals
excerpt: Russia’s teenage tennis star Mirra Andreeva has won her first WTA Finals crown without dropping a set against her Ukrainian rival Elina Svitolina, who did not shake hands with the champion at the end ...
body_text:
Russia’s teenage tennis star Mirra Andreeva has won her first WTA Finals crown without dropping a set against her Ukrainian rival Elina Svitolina, who did not shake hands with the champion at the end of a one-sided match in Indian Wells, California.

After her 7-5, 6-3 victory on Sunday, Andreeva, who turned 19 in April during a successful year that saw her win her first Grand Slam and ascend to number two in the world, took home $3.37m and a one-of-a-kind, ultraviolet purple Mercedes-Benz convertible car at the season-ending championships. Now, all she needs is a driver’s licence.

She happily got behind the wheel after the car was driven onto the court at the Indian Wells Tennis Garden.

“This is an amazing motivation for me to get my driver’s licence as fast as I can,” she said. “If not, then look, I have five people on my team. I’m going to be a passenger princess forever. That’s also an option for me.”

After match point, Andreeva ran to hug coach Conchita Martinez in the stands. Svitolina, a 32-year-old mother, sat down in her chair.

The players did not take part in the traditional post-match handshake or pose for photos together before the match. Svitolina and others from her country have refused to shake hands with players from Russia and Belarus since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 in line with a policy set by the Ukrainian Tennis Federation.

Svitolina didn’t mention Andreeva in her post-match comments to the crowd, which included several fans waving Ukrainian flags.

Later, she said, “I couldn’t thank the people of Ukraine enough for coming to watch my matches, to watch at home.”

Andreeva publicly congratulated Svitolina for what she called an “amazing” season.

“You’re an amazing mom to come back and do this. It’s super hard,” she said. “I just wish you the best of luck for the next season.”

Svitolina nodded without expression from her seat.

“I put everything out there, and she played incredible,” Svitolina said later.

Andreeva became the 11th player to win the finals without losing a set, joining, among others, Chris Evert, Martina Navratilova and Serena Williams, all of whom did it multiple times.

“I’m super privileged to put my name in that group,” she said.

She jumped in the air when Svitolina netted an easy smash on the second match point.

Andreeva is also the second youngest player to win the WTA Finals behind her compatriot Maria Sharapova, who won at 17.

During the awards presentation, she wore a jacket with the phrase “I want to thank myself” stamped on the front, and then she did just that.

“I want to thank myself for always doing the hard work, for never quitting, for always believing in myself, for not taking the days off, for working every day and for committing to what I have to do,” she said. “Just thanks to myself without any reason.”

In doubles, Katerina Siniakova and Taylor Townsend beat the Italian duo of Sara Errani and Jasmine Paolini 6-4, 6-3.

It was the sixth title of the year for the Czech-American team of Siniakova and Townsend, who also won the French Open and US Open.

Svitolina said she would return to Ukraine next week, pledging to continue supporting her country through donations, her foundation and the platform she has built in tennis.

“It’s been almost five years. I’ve always been supportive of the army and the soldiers,” Svitolina told reporters. “They always support me by watching the matches, and I have lots of friends that are serving the country.”

Svitolina, the world number six, said sport could offer people a release from the strain and uncertainty of daily life during wartime.

“For me it’s all about the spirit, the spirit of the people,” she said. “I’m very happy that I can bring a little happiness to the people of Ukraine.”

“Sports in general and in Ukraine especially really unite people for one goal – to win.”

title: The Red Sea cannot be secured without restoring the Yemeni state
excerpt: For a decade, the Yemen civil war was treated as a regional issue, confined to the southern part of the Arabian Peninsula. But as escalations in 2024-2025 and this year have made clear, the conflict n...
body_text:
For a decade, the Yemen civil war was treated as a regional issue, confined to the southern part of the Arabian Peninsula. But as escalations in 2024-2025 and this year have made clear, the conflict now directly affects the whole world, disrupting global trade and navigation and impacting the strategic interests of every major power.

The Houthis’ ability, with Iranian backing, to endanger maritime transit through the Bab al-Mandeb strait, one of the world’s most critical maritime corridors, is not an isolated military development.

It resulted directly from the collapse of Yemeni state institutions, the dwindling international support for the legitimate government, the proliferation of armed factions and the conflicting regional agendas.

As the past few months have demonstrated, the security of navigation cannot be restored with aircraft carriers and naval task forces alone. A long-term solution necessitates first recognising and then addressing the root causes of the Yemen crisis.

The international community, now facing the consequences of Houthi attacks on commercial vessels, did almost nothing to prevent Yemen’s disintegration. Some of its actions even contributed to the Houthis’ seizure of Sanaa in September 2014.

The Houthi coup marked a decisive turning point, ending the post-2011 transition and opening the way for a parallel armed authority with its own political project that controls strategic territory, including the approaches to Bab al-Mandeb and the highlands overlooking the Red Sea.

Most dangerously, the Houthis inherited the residual capabilities of a state whose military was once ranked the fifth most heavily armed in the Arab world.

This combination of territorial control, inherited state and military capacity, and external sponsorship has made the Houthi threat more serious and more durable than that ever posed by ISIS or al-Qaeda.

And yet, the international community has not treated the Houthis as seriously as it did ISIS and al-Qaeda, nor has it placed the restoration of Yemeni national institutions as top priority. It has approached the Houthis as a force that could be contained, negotiated with, or instrumentalised.

Instead of defending the Yemeni state, the international community settled for temporary understandings and political pressure. One example is the 2018 Stockholm Agreement on the strategic port city of Hodeidah, which secured a ceasefire, mutual redeployment, and UN-supervised security and financial arrangements directing port revenues to the Central Bank rather than to the Houthis. Yet, the deal entrenched the Houthis as the de facto authority over the port and the city as a whole, leaving the power imbalance tilted in their favour; it is highly unpopular among anti-Houthi forces.

In 2021, the Houthis managed to solidify their grip on Hodeidah governorate after the inexplicable withdrawal of the Joint Forces on the Western Coast, a coalition of forces fighting on the side of the internationally recognised Yemeni government.

Neither the Joint Forces nor the regional coalition supporting them had notified the Yemeni government or the UN of their movements; civilians in these areas were told 24 hours prior, which did not give them enough time to evacuate.

The episode exposed not just the failure of the Stockholm Agreement – something acknowledged by the UN Panel of Experts on Yemen – but also the failure of the anti-Houthi front, which faced multiple military decision-making centres, inadequate coordination with the government and growing contradictions within the regional coalition.

Rather than building a national army under the legitimate government through the defence ministry, the coalition allowed numerous local formations to emerge outside the state’s chain of command. This was reflected in the Emirati backing for the separatist Southern Transitional Council and Saudi Arabia’s divergent priorities.

By empowering armed formations that refuse to submit to the very state they claim to restore, Yemen’s backers left the anti-Houthi camp divided, allowing the Houthis to consolidate their gains and avoid a decisive confrontation with a united Yemeni army.

As a result, today, the region and the world face a militia that has captured a state and is armed with drones, ballistic and potentially hypersonic missiles. It is controlling coastline beside a major waterway and is using geography as an instrument of pressure and blackmail.

The international response has been a military deployment at sea. However sophisticated, naval deployments and maritime operations may intercept missiles but cannot deliver a lasting solution, since they leave untouched the conditions that allow an armed group to launch attacks from Yemeni territory.

Treating the Houthi threat as a discrete maritime problem addresses only its symptoms while leaving its causes in place. Red Sea security cannot be separated from the security of the states that border it.

Yemen has nearly 2,500km of coastline along the Arabian Sea, the Red Sea, and the Gulf of Aden, and overlooks Bab al-Mandeb. Any serious strategy must treat Yemen’s crisis as one of state, sovereignty and institutions rather than a contest between rival parties.

That requires restoring the primacy of the national-state project, supporting legitimate institutions, unifying military and security forces under a single national command, ending the multiplicity of power centres, and reaching a political settlement only after armed groups, represented by the Houthis, have been broken and defeated, so that a stable state becomes possible.

All Gulf states, including the UAE, must recognise that their own security and stability depend on restoring the Yemeni state and supporting its military and security institutions. Accommodating or empowering armed groups, such as the Houthis and the Southern Transitional Council, can only fuel instability.

The international community too must recognise that restoring the Yemeni state is not a purely Yemeni concern. It is in the strategic interest of the whole world.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

title: ‘It’s like the 16th-century version of doomscrolling’: the Book of Miracles may fetch £1m at auction
excerpt:
Exclusive: Public institutions get first chance to bid for rare ‘wonderbook’ of apocalyptic visions and extreme weather

In one illustration, five suns blaze down on Leipzig in 1551. In another, blood...
body_text:
Exclusive: Public institutions get first chance to bid for rare ‘wonderbook’ of apocalyptic visions and extreme weather

In one illustration, five suns blaze down on Leipzig in 1551. In another, blood rain falls on Rome in 1456. In a third scene, dated 1552, monstrous hailstones batter the Dutch city of Dordrecht during a storm so fierce people feared Judgment Day had come.

Created during the mid-16th century, when earthquakes, storms, floods and other extreme weather events were often interpreted as ominous warnings from God, the Book of Miracles contains 167 paintings of apocalyptic visions, celestial wonders and meteorological phenomena.

It is the only known copy. To this day, no one is sure why it was created.

Now, public institutions will have their first chance to bid for the Book of Miracles since scholars learned it existed. It is expected to fetch between £700,000 and £1m when it is auctioned in London on 10 December, as the star lot of the Christie’s valuable books and manuscripts sale.

Members of the public will also have a rare opportunity to see it in person for six days before it goes under the hammer.

For nearly half a millennium, scholars were unaware of its existence. Found in the library of a small baroque castle in southern Germany nearly 20 years ago, the manuscript, which from 1550s Augsburg, was put up for auction alongside the castle’s furniture, carpets and tankards in 2008 and sold for just over £100,000.

Shortly after the sale, the manuscript entered the private collection of Mickey Cartin, one of Connecticut’s biggest contemporary art collectors.

Eugenio Donadoni, Christie’s international specialist in medieval and Renaissance manuscripts, said the book was an “exceptionally rare” German wonderbook.

“German wonderbooks functioned as the sensationalist mass media of their day,” he said. “They were used by Lutheran theologians such as Martin Luther and Philip Melanchthon to further their Protestant eschatology, but crucially – with all the depictions of comets, cosmological events, natural disasters, all verified by witnesses, with exact dates and geographic coordinates – they laid early foundations for empirical observation and reporting. They mark a shift from medieval to Enlightenment.”

He expects the sale will attract collectors of both historic and modern art because some of the scenes, which are painted in watercolour and gouache, are “super surrealist … almost Dalí-esque”.

“If it weren’t for the little captions, which are obviously 16th-century German, some of them look so vividly modern … it’s really jaw-dropping,” Donadoni said.

The scenes depicted include a plague of locusts arriving in Poland on a “terrible wind” in 1527 and the North Sea flooding the coast of Frisia – in what is now the Netherlands and Germany – in 1230.

Other pictures are of fiery comets and eclipses, while scholars think an illustration of “wondrous dragons” flying across the sky over Bavaria in 1533 depicts the northern lights.

Underneath each scene, a German picture caption describes what is happening and where and when the event took place.

“All of these events are portentous,” said Donadoni. “The artists of the Book of Miracles, relying on contemporary broadsheets, chronicles and histories, have condensed into pictorial form the concerns of an age that was gripped by an anxiety – and learned curiosity – about the future.”

The book records how uneasy people felt about climatic anomalies at a time of doctrinal disunity, when there was growing interest in documenting and cataloguing visible, tangible scientific phenomena, he said.

“It’s really fascinating … it is a window into how Europeans were dealing with the impending end of the world, political uncertainty and extreme – and strange – weather events.”

The five suns over Leipzig, for example, is thought to depict the optical illusion of a parhelion, more commonly known as a sun dog. “You see in the sky various different rings of light and it looks like suns,” Donadoni said.

“Blood rain” occurs when high concentrations of red-coloured dust particles, usually from the Sahara, mix with water droplets in rain clouds. “Many of these things have actual rational scientific explanations to them,” Donadoni said.

He said he imagined that leafing through the pages of the book in the 1550s was similar to bingeing on bad news on social media today: “I think it could be a little like the 16th-century version of doomscrolling.”

In this way, the book straddles a momentous turning point in history. “We’re right at that period where the superstition of the middle ages turns into the age of scientific discovery,” Donadoni said.

Till-Holger Borchert, the director of the Suermondt Ludwig Museum in Aachen, has studied the manuscript and said the first time he saw it, his reaction was: “Wow”. “It’s one of a kind,” he said. “It grabs you by your heart or your soul or your belly.”

He said he thought £1m was a “very conservative estimate” of its value. “It [the final price] could possibly be much more,” he said.

A facsimile of the manuscript was published in 2013 that got people “really excited” about it, Borchert added, and since then the Book of Miracles has become “a kind of icon for people who are interested in apocalyptic things”. It would be wrong to value it merely as an historical document: “It’s more than that. It speaks to us, to our generation.”

title: Andy Burnham to say Brexit ‘has not worked’ and he will sign new deal with EU
excerpt:
Prime minister is to meet European leaders at summit this week and secure agreements that ‘could raise GDP by 0.4%’

Andy Burnham will say on Monday that Brexit “has not worked” and that he will sign ...
body_text:
Prime minister is to meet European leaders at summit this week and secure agreements that ‘could raise GDP by 0.4%’

Andy Burnham will say on Monday that Brexit “has not worked” and that he will sign a new deal with the EU.

It is the latest in a string of comments by the prime minister criticising Brexit, after he told the Welsh Labour conference on Saturday that the UK has “lost more than we gained” through leaving the EU.

Burnham is due to meet European leaders at a summit this week and secure agreements that he says could raise GDP by 0.4% – about £17bn – including on food and farming, emissions trading and a youth mobility scheme.

Speaking at the lord mayor’s banquet in the City of London, Burnham is expected to argue that Boris Johnson’s promise to take back control was not delivered, and that the country was left with a needlessly hard Brexit that created barriers for businesses and damaged its economic potential.

“It’s like the Emperor’s New Clothes – where no one is prepared to say the obvious truth. Well, I say it as I see it. And to be frank, the emperor has nothing on,” Burnham will say. “The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we gained.”

Burnham is to say he will sign an agreement with the EU, so long as it:

Is consistent with the Labour manifesto and the government’s red lines.

It improves the Brexit deal and brings it closer to what people thought they were voting for in 2016.

And it passes the so-called “Makerfield test” by delivering real, tangible improvements in people’s everyday lives.

“This is a win-win,” Burnham is expected to say. “It illustrates our new approach. Not adversarial. No longer burning bridges – but being constructive and positive, showing that we can come together to confront shared challenges.”

However, the EU relations minister, Hamish Falconer, told the BBC on Sunday that the UK could have a “voice in the room” under a new deal with the bloc, but no vote on EU food policies.

He added there could well be an “exit clause” in case a future UK government reversed the closer alignment, explaining that the EU was “worried” about the possibility of a future Reform or Conservative government undoing the agreement.

The BBC understands the clause is a result of EU concerns about the possible cost of having to rebuild facilities for border food safety checks which were put in place after Brexit.

Meanwhile, Johnson, the former Conservative prime minister who resigned over Partygate in 2022, has said Britain would “absolutely” vote for Brexit again if Burnham forced another vote on the issue.

He told the Telegraph: “It is madness to escalate the Brexit issue as your political priority.

“He will impale himself and his party on this point, and he needs to move off it because he won’t win – because the reality is that people are not fools.”

title: Ma Wee Tin O’Shortbreid: a journey in search of the real Highlands
excerpt: Ma Wee Tin o’ Shortbreid began as a cautionary note: don’t make the Highlands look like a shortbread tin. Then Dougie Wallace shot a Chinese tourist beneath a wee umbrella, and the warning became the ...
body_text:
Ma Wee Tin o’ Shortbreid began as a cautionary note: don’t make the Highlands look like a shortbread tin. Then Dougie Wallace shot a Chinese tourist beneath a wee umbrella, and the warning became the title

Growing up in Scotland, our family was one of many who kept their photographs in an old shortbread tin. The lid usually showed a castle beside a loch, a stag, a Highland coo and plenty of tartan. It was always sunny.

Ma Wee Tin o’ Shortbreid is Scots for “my little tin of shortbread”. The title started as a warning to myself: don’t make the Highlands look like a tin of shortbread.

Then, at Eilean Donan Castle, about as biscuit-tin lid as it gets, I photographed a Chinese tourist under a wee umbrella, remaking the view for her own photograph.

Yellow backpacks and trekking poles rest on benches, with Ben Nevis rising behind

They were shot to extinction in Britain, the last one in Shetland in 1918. Brought back from Norway in the 1970s. Now they are one of the island’s biggest draws. A bird once shot on sight is part of the sales pitch. The Scotland on the lid promises wilderness and wildlife. The real one comes with binoculars and a long wait.

(L-R): Isle of Mull. Out of the camper van, looking for white-tailed eagles and a tourist photographs the Scottish Highlands through a coach window.

One of the buses that leave Edinburgh every morning to do the Highlands in a day. Most of the day is spent on the bus. Glencoe seen through the window of a Heilan coo (Highland cow).

Glencoe, Highlands. Two women with a geological map. There was a supervolcano here about 420m years ago. In 1909 it became the textbook case for how one collapses. The glaciers finished the job. The forces that shaped Scotland. No, not the English.

Some of that emptiness was made. Highland regiments fought the empire’s wars while the glens were cleared for sheep and sporting estates. The view people come for was somebody’s home.

Callanish standing stones, Isle of Lewis. They went up 5,000 years ago, older than Stonehenge.

Visitors arrive looking for a Scotland they’ve seen on screens. They come for wilderness and find a queue, a coach park and a wait for somebody to move out of the frame.

Isle of Skye. Highland cattle, one of the oldest registered breeds in the world, with a herd book going back to 1885. Bred to stand outside all winter without a hat. Even the coos get a souvenir.

At the famous sites, I kept noticing how many visitors were Chinese and Indian, from countries Britain once ruled, traded with or fought. They were photographing the familiar symbols of old Scotland. This time, Scotland was the attraction, and they were the ones behind the camera.

Kilt Rock, Isle of Skye. Named because the cliffs look like a pleated kilt. Nobody believes you’ve been to Scotland without a soaking-wet picture.

Even the weather is for sale. Cool air and rain have become part of the escape. In what felt like London’s hottest summer ever, Londoners drove north to find the cold and wet, though a week of horizontal rain may test the sales pitch.

Most Highland roads are one-lane wide with passing places. Out on the open hill, there’s often no fence between the sheep and the road. All the way from Frankfurt to give way to a sheep.

I’m making these photographs on repeated trips in my camper van: 60 days and 5,000 miles so far, a good part of it stuck behind a motorhome. I’ve been to Skye five times and driven the North Coast 500 (NC500) road in both directions. The project grew out of Weather Permitting, my photographs of Scotland’s ski centres.

Reaching the wilderness usually means driving to it, on the same narrow roads as residents, deliveries, coaches and motorhomes. An empty road makes a good advert. Everyone driving down it makes a different picture.

Ben Nevis, near Fort William. Scotland has a daily midge forecast, one to five. People swear by Avon Skin So Soft as a repellent. Only the females bite, while the males feed on flowers. When one finds you, she sends for her pals. Tiny, relentless, and missing from the shortbread tin.

Blair Castle, Blair Atholl, Perthshire. Home of the Atholl Highlanders, the only remaining private army in Europe. One of the first castles to open to the public, in 1936. Anyone can be chief now. Right: Eilean Donan Castle, near Kyle of Lochalsh. The kitchen is set up as it was in the 1930s, halfway through getting a banquet ready. The cook’s been at the same pot since 1932.

Dunvegan Castle, Isle of Skye, home of the MacLeod chiefs for 800 years and the oldest continuously inhabited castle in Scotland. There are quite enough portraits in here already. They’ve never had as many followers.

Strathdon, Aberdeenshire, 7.30am. The Lonach Highlanders set off on their six-mile march to the Lonach Highland Gathering, same as every August since the 1830s. Eight-foot pikes, a dram and a shout of ‘Ho, ho Lonach’ at six houses on the way. The pikes get heavier. Right: After Culloden, the Dress Act of 1746 made wearing the kilt a crime, and it stayed that way until 1782. Now they play fitba in them. Jumpers for goalposts. Sporrans for shin pads.

Braemar, Aberdeenshire, the morning of the Braemar Gathering, a few miles up the road from Balmoral. Queen Victoria came in 1848 and royalty has been turning up ever since. About 17,000 people come for the caber, the pipe bands and a look at the king. Nobody in the glen would dream of telling the drum major he’s overdressed.

The Lonach Highland Gathering. Highland fling. The proper one is danced on the spot, on the balls of the feet, without ever moving off it. The ladies are about to find out what a true Scotsman wears under his kilt.

Loch Morlich, near Aviemore. Britain’s highest beach, on the road to the Cairngorm ski slopes. It is 300 metres up and in 2009 it became the first freshwater loch to win a Seaside award. Wetsuits are recommended.

Cairngorm Mountain ski resort, near Aviemore. The kettle goes on in the back of a camper van as the snow comes down. Tropical aquarium inside. Snowstorm outside.

Sauna na Mara, Carbost, Isle of Skye. Carbost is better known for the Talisker distillery up the road but the wood-fired sauna on the shore has become part of the island’s new wellness trail, alongside the cold-water swimmers, the boutique bothies and the queue for the same photo at the Fairy Pools. One way or another, you’ll warm up.

Isle of Lewis. Crofters have had the right to cut peat for their own fire since 1886. Not to sell it. Peat grows about a millimetre a year. A winter’s fire takes thousands of years to make and an afternoon to cut. It heats the house and flavours the whisky.

Newtonmore, Highlands. Shut that windae, you’re letting the heat oot.

Isle of Lewis. A traditional dwelling called a blackhouse, with its roof tied down with ropes and stones against Atlantic gales. Family lived at one end, cattle at the other. People were still living in them on Lewis until 1974. Now you can book one for the week. The dog hasn’t been offered a room.

Tourism brings work and money. It also needs people who can afford to live close enough to keep the place running. Between No Motorhomes and No More Homes, it’s getting harder for anyone to stay.

Isle of Benbecula, Outer Hebrides. Eriskay ponies once carried the crofters’ peat and seaweed. By the 1970s, the breed was down to 20 mares and one stallion. The big grey is an Eriskay, bred with a waterproof coat. The wee one is a miniature shetland pony. Had to buy its own.

Ceannabeinne beach, near Durness, Sutherland, on the NC500. Nobody on the sand. Everybody on the bend.

The NC500 was launched in 2015 to sell 516 miles of empty road. It worked. Camper van life has its own pitch: freedom, independence, a new view every morning. In practice, it depends on ferry bookings, fresh water, waste points and somewhere you’re allowed to stop. Freedom, it turns out, needs a booking reference.

Travelling this way, I’m part of what I’m photographing, on the same roads, ferries and overnight stops as everyone else. The open road can still end at a full layby or a No Motorhomes sign. Passing places become car parks and viewpoints become campsites.

Durness, Sutherland, on the NC500. Everybody parks to face the sea. You used to be able to see it from here.

Durness, Sutherland, on the NC500, about as far north-west as the mainland goes. Nothing between here and the Atlantic to slow the wind down. The duvet’s making a break for it.

Over July and August one year, about 14,000 motorhomes and nearly 11,000 tents pitched up within five miles of Durness. A few hundred people live there … The NC500 has been a named tourist route for just over a decade. What will it look like in another 10 or 20 years? Part of making these photographs is recording this moment, before we find out.

Isle of Skye. Two Highlanders. Only one of them’s been on a shortbread tin.

The pictures are about the gap between Scotland as advertised and the place people find. I set out not to photograph the shortbread tin. I kept finding people trying to climb inside it.

title: UK blood services issue urgent appeal for donations as winter approaches
excerpt:
Supplies are low and reserves of certain types are half of what the UK needs, officials say

UK blood services have issued an urgent appeal for 150,000 donations to help the NHS cope with the increase...
body_text:
Supplies are low and reserves of certain types are half of what the UK needs, officials say

UK blood services have issued an urgent appeal for 150,000 donations to help the NHS cope with the increase in demand that occurs during the winter.

Supplies of blood have run particularly low, with reserves of certain blood types only half of what is considered necessary, officials say.

They include supplies of O negative, B negative, O positive and RO blood. People of black heritage have also been asked to donate to help the NHS treat people with sickle cell disease.

The health service needs 5,000 donors every day – who either give blood already or are new volunteers – from now until the new year in order to ensure hospitals have enough for patients. That is because blood has a shelf life of 35 days and platelets of just seven days.

Blood service officials want people to fill 150,000 donation appointments over the coming weeks and help boost what they stress are “life-saving supplies” of vital products.

Each donation takes an hour and can help save three lives, they say.

Winter’s cold weather brings two challenges for blood supply agencies. The greater prevalence of colds, coughs and respiratory illnesses such as flu stops people who are unwell from donating.

It can also leave people with long-term conditions, including sickle cell disease and cancer, needing to receive more blood or transfusions of platelets to safeguard their health.

“Right now, as we move into winter, there is an urgent need to boost our life-saving blood, platelet and plasma supplies”, said Gerry Gogarty, the director of blood and plasma supply at NHS Blood and Transplant.

“With patients reliant on regular transfusions, particularly vulnerable to colds and respiratory illnesses, it is vital that we stay well stocked to ensure the blood is always there when it is needed.”

Earlier this month, the Scottish National Blood Transfusion Service announced its first amber alert for O blood types. Stocks had dropped to “unprecedented low levels” because of a shortage of donors and greater use of the blood type over recent months, it explained.

Health chiefs also want to ramp up supplies of blood plasma. That is needed to make medicines for people with serious immune conditions, which become harder to manage in winter.

Bigger donation centres in town and city centres offer the most appointments, especially for first-time donors and those with common blood types, Gogarty said.

He asked those who cannot find an appointment immediately to keep checking back to help take up last-minute availability or cancellations.

title: How Russia is preparing Iran for the next escalation
excerpt:
Senior Fellow at the Department of War Studies at King’s College London.

This week, there has been some cautious optimism about a de-escalation in the US-Israel war on Iran. Qatari and Pakistani medi...
body_text:
Senior Fellow at the Department of War Studies at King’s College London.

This week, there has been some cautious optimism about a de-escalation in the US-Israel war on Iran. Qatari and Pakistani mediators have intensified efforts to conclude a deal between the warring sides after a massive military build-up in the region raised fears of a renewed kinetic phase of the conflict.

There are various factors that have played into the decision of US President Donald Trump to hold off on new attacks for now. One of them is certainly Iran’s ability to see an assault coming and retaliate with precision – a capability that is likely made possible by Russian military-grade geospatial and signals intelligence.

For eight months now, Project AURORAH, which I founded, has followed the trajectories of Russian spy satellites. It has identified at least 20 Russian spacecraft in the Kosmos-2600 series, 18 of which can be tracked.

I focus on this group because it includes Russia’s newest and most manoeuvrable military reconnaissance satellites. They can provide military cartographic reconnaissance of installations and terrain, as well as optical imagery, radar observation, and signals intelligence collection, including radar and other radio frequency emissions and military communications activity.

The satellites I have followed cover an area that extends from Syria, Lebanon and Israel to Jordan, Saudi Arabia, the wider Arabian Peninsula, Iraq and Iran, including both Bab al-Mandeb and the Strait of Hormuz. They circle Earth approximately every 95 minutes, with roughly three to four relevant regional passes daily, depending on viewing geometry.

I observed how selected manoeuvrable satellites were repositioned so that they would pass directly or almost directly over military and infrastructure targets in the region. The entire constellation of satellites was not moved, just specific spacecraft, which would improve the timing and quality of coverage over relevant targets.

These Russian satellites could be observed passing over targets before they were struck and then again after they were struck, presumably to assess the damage. The same pattern occurred repeatedly before and after Iranian attacks.

Given the precision with which Iran was able to strike United States and Gulf military and civilian targets, my conclusion is that Russia provided the Iranian army with the geospatial intelligence it needed to carry out these attacks.

The problem for the US is that such intelligence capabilities can be used not just for target selection, but also for monitoring a military build-up.

As US aircraft are being repositioned, naval forces redistributed and military infrastructure reinforced in the region, Russian satellites can provide a clear picture of these movements and the intensity of military communications, including where the communications come from, when activity increases, and how the pattern changes.

It is possible that some spy satellites can also listen to military communications, although it is unlikely they can intercept every message.

The intelligence collected can be passed to Iranian intelligence to help Iranian leaders protect their forces, keep their command system operating, and prepare their response before fighting begins.

Therefore, Iranian access to Russian satellite data collection would complicate US efforts to combine offensive readiness with protection against retaliation. One solution is to move formations farther from Iranian weapons to reduce their immediate exposure, but also to alter the distribution of combat power Tehran is observing.

Russian assistance would also give Iran early warning capabilities for attacks originating from outside the region. During Operation Midnight Hammer in June 2025, B-2 Spirit bombers flew from continental US to strike Iranian nuclear facilities. Tehran knows that there can be another such assault on deeply buried facilities and therefore can use Russian satellite capabilities to monitor for early signs of it.

Needless to say, apart from preparedness to receive an attack, access to Russian satellite intelligence is likely playing a central role in preparations for retaliation in the region. As Iranian leaders have warned, the danger extends to refineries, export terminals, desalination plants and power stations.

In other words, if Trump reverses his decision and decides to attack, Iran will not only be ready for what the US Army does, but it will also be able to exact a devastating blow to the region.

Damage would disrupt civilian water and electricity supplies and transmit the effects into international energy markets. Saudi Arabia’s position as the world’s largest crude-oil exporter gives its export infrastructure particular global significance. Neighbouring Arab Gulf countries would face these consequences regardless of their influence over the decision to resume war.

It is important to consider that by providing Iran with such space intelligence capabilities, Russia retains significant leverage. Moscow is able to strengthen or restrain Tehran by controlling intelligence access without entering the conflict directly.

Russia’s willingness to share satellite data collection will inevitably impact future US operations. The US Army must now assume that major force movements, military build-ups and electronic activity can be observed and rapidly relayed to an adversary. This reduces operational surprise and requires greater dispersion, emission control and rapid relocation.

The consequences also extend beyond this war. Last month, a Russian Kosmos-series satellite approached a Finnish commercial satellite, possibly rehearsing an attack. This incident indicates that conflict on the ground can expand into space, potentially disrupting civilian and military satellite infrastructure. In present and future wars, we may very well see an escalation into space.

The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

title: Monday briefing: The many stages of the UK-EU relationship – and what’s next
excerpt:
In today’s newsletter: From situationship to a possible makeup, a look at the evolving relationship, and the bloc’s big feelings about the future

Good morning. Ahead of the hotly anticipated UK-EU su...
body_text:
In today’s newsletter: From situationship to a possible makeup, a look at the evolving relationship, and the bloc’s big feelings about the future

Good morning. Ahead of the hotly anticipated UK-EU summit this Friday, Andy Burnham is expected to make the reset of our relationship with Europe the pivotal theme of his white-tie speech at the lord mayor’s banquet in London tonight.

The prospect of closer ties – and the possibility of going “all the way” to reversing Brexit – has been met with jubilation and relief in some quarters and vehement opposition in others, while around Westminster and across the media the psychodrama has been spiralling for weeks.

At this point, I’m reminded of that Robert Burns couplet: “O wad some Pow’r the giftie gie us / To see oursels as ithers see us!” What does the EU think about all this? Are they ready to reverse what leading figures have repeatedly described as a colossal act of self-harm? Or are they viewing this latest iteration with bombastic side-eye? I posed these questions to Jennifer Rankin, the Guardian’s Brussels correspondent. First the headlines.

UK news | A woman who alleges she was raped by Russell Brand when she was 16 has waived her right to anonymity to campaign for a staggered age of consent, which would make it illegal for adults over a certain age to have sex with 16- and 17-year-olds.

Youth unemployment | Andy Burnham has pledged to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment before a watershed review, promising “a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world”.

Environment | The strongest El Niño in centuries has added urgency to UN climate talks in Turkey as vulnerable countries face “compounding” crises. In other Cop31 news, queer and gay protesters defied a crackdown on LGBTQ+ rights in Turkey to lead a civil society climate march.

UK news | Two people aged 22 and 23 have died after their car was hit by a BMW being pursued by police. West Yorkshire police said four people had been arrested and appealed for witnesses to come forward.

Air transport | The Trump administration says Friday’s four-hour nationwide Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) ground stop that delayed or cancelled thousands of flight stemmed from routine maintenance. The US transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, blamed prior presidents and Congress for the stoppage.

Ahead of the summit, the pro-Brexit polity has been in broadcast mode: headlines from the past few days include: “Burnham’s plot to rejoin the EU would leave the average UK household £6,500 poorer” (Express); “Taxpayers funding pro-EU university courses” (Sunday Telegraph); “Staggering cost of PM’s EU reset” (Daily Mail).

Stay Out, a new campaign against rejoining the European Union, launched last week. While the guy you really want to hear from right now – David Cameron, the prime minister who lost the 2016 Brexit referendum – has insisted the UK’s problems have nothing to do with its exit from the EU.

Even within the Labour fold, there are rumblings of unease from MPs and unions.

But the one-day summit in Brussels this Friday does not include any formal discussion of rejoining: instead, the EU and UK hope to sign deals on food and drink, emissions trading and the youth experience scheme (a work and study exchange programme).

Still, the mood music is upbeat. Back in September, when Burnham first opened the door to a Brexit reversal, French president Emmanual Macron responded: “welcome back.” while Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez said: “Spain would welcome Britain’s return with open arms.”

The enthusiasm is genuine, says Jennifer. Indeed, some European diplomats have told her the technicalities could be wrapped up within a year because the UK remains closely aligned with the bloc in so many areas. “It would be such a vote of confidence in the European project for a country to decide to return after voting to leave”.

Situationship: what’s at stake at this week’s summit?

Though Burnham has predicted “some long nights” of negotiation this week, Jennifer says there’s optimism on each side as the first two deals on food and drink and emissions trading were largely agreed.

There are two sticking points with the youth exchange deal. First, the Home Office wants to limit numbers to the UK to keep migration figures low. Second, there’s disagreement over whether those students would pay UK domestic rates of tuition fees or the international rate, which is four or five times higher for some courses.

The UK is offering concessions on tuition fees if it can join Made in Europe, the EU legislation designed to protect domestic manufacturing from cheap Chinese competition. But the EU says it can’t make a deal on Made in Europe this week, because the law is still at a draft stage.

And here’s where it gets complicated. The European Commission has proposed delaying an agreement on tuition fees for six months, which could allow time to get the UK into Made in Europe, a diplomatic win for Britain. But there’s pushback from member states who want to pin down the UK on tuition fees this week. “This is a real priority for the EU, in almost emotional terms,” Jennifer says. “Lots of EU officials and diplomats studied in the UK, or their children did, and they felt this was one of the big losses of Brexit, that these person-to-person links were being eroded.”

On-again, off-again: what else could get in the way of closer working?

In play at Friday’s summit will also be a future deal on Britain’s return to the EU’s internal electricity market and a joint migration pact, with the UK pushing for access to EU crime databases to tackle the small boats crisis.

Member states are already working hard to smooth things out on the electricity front, to stop it becoming a sticking point. A couple of weeks ago, Jennifer reported on leaders from Germany, Denmark and elsewhere calling for deeper cooperation on clean energy – which she reads as an attempt to head off a row about how much the UK should contribute to EU cohesion funds for the evident privilege of cutting red tape, easing trade and, ultimately, reducing costs.

A similar row over UK contributions scuppered negotiations last year on our entry into a €150bn EU defence fund.

It could also be a challenge for the UK to realign with the EU on farming, after changing to a payment model that puts more emphasis on delivering environmental benefits. And past UK governments have been lukewarm about EU AI regulation, devised post Brexit.

Conscious partnership: will the EU welcome future closeness this week?

I learned long ago there’s no such thing as a stupid question, so I ask mine now: will there be a moment on Friday when Ursula von der Leyen offers the equivalent of Macron’s “welcome back”? Will there be a “just give us six months to sort out the paperwork Andy” vibe?

The European Commission president is, by nature, a cautious politician, Jennifer tells me, so she doesn’t expect anything so specific. “I’m sure she – and António Costa, the European Council president – will get asked about it at the press conference, and they’ll want to send a signal about the UK being welcome to rejoin.”

But behind closed doors, in Brussels and other capitals, what Jennifer hears repeatedly is that it’s up to the UK to decide what it wants. And, while the prospect of Brexiteer Nigel Farage in Downing Street has faded in recent months, there remains a deal of caution about the vicissitudes of UK politics. “Now the Burnham government is exploring the options, but there’s also an awareness that you could have a very different government in a few years’ time,” she says.

It’s not you, it’s me: what else is Europe worrying about?

The EU and its member states are preoccupied with far weightier problems: the war in Ukraine (Volodymyr Zelenskyy attends every EU summit), the rise in support for the far right, street protests, hybrid threats from Russia, a trade deficit with China that has reached a staggering €1bn a day in 2026.

“There are so many other issues crowding on the agenda,” says Jennifer. So it’s not all about us? “That’s actually been the theme of my decade of reporting from Brussels,” she says with a laugh.

There’s profound concern about the prospect of Marine Le Pen winning the French presidential elections next year, which could tip the bloc into a crisis if she pursues her resolutely anti-EU agenda, which includes reducing France’s substantial contribution to the EU budget.

Beyond that, there’s a broader question about increasingly divided and unstable politics across member states. “Every single member state has to agree to the UK’s re-entry,” Jennifer reminds me. “Who knows what the EU will look like in 2030 when Britain could be having a rejoin referendum?”

Tuesday | The work and pensions secretary Alan Milburn’s long-awaited review into why increasing numbers of young people are falling out of work and education, is expected to be released.

Thursday | German chancellor Friedrich Merz, French president Emmanuel Macron and UK prime minister Andy Burnham will be among around 20 heads of state meeting in Berlin to discuss defence funding for Ukraine, and to establish a unified position on future peace negotiations in its war with Russia.

Friday | This marks last day of the world’s biggest annual climate conference, Cop31, in Turkey, with final negotiations taking place.

With a stellar range of interviews, Nadia Khomami is excellent on 2000s pop culture, and how openly horrible it was to women. Poppy Noor, newsletters team

Emma Beddington’s piece on why gen Xer seem to have worse mental and physical health than boomers is a must-read. Poppy

Amelia Gentleman’s report over the weekend on two very different rape trials and what happened in each of them is a difficult read – but enlightening about all of the ways culture has (and has not) changed since Russell Brand’s prominence. Poppy

Football | England risked throwing away a three-goal lead against Spain after Elliot Anderson was sent off, but held on for a thrilling 3-2 win in Madrid, which Thomas Tuchel hailed as a statement result and the best performance of his tenure.

Cricket | Tom Banton’s century led England to emphatic win, with 135 runs, in second ODI amid Australian soap opera.

Rugby union | Tries from Matt Fagerson and Jack Dempsey gave Scotland a 15-12 win against Australia in the Nations Championship at Murrayfield

“PM vows early years interventions will tackle youth joblessness crisis”, is the Guardian’s front page today.

The i Paper leads with “Pressure grows for new consent law to protect teenagers from adult predators”, Metro has “Rethink on the age of consent”, the Sun writes “Brand’s rant from prison”.

The Telegraph says “Johnson: Britain would back Brexit again”, the Express writes “Brexit U-turn means ‘more asylum seekers’”. The Times has “Zero-hours ban to cost billions”, the Mail has “£80,000 a day spent ferrying migrants around”, the Mirror’s splash is “Dying in the dark”, and the FT’s is “Nvidia scandal spurs drive to choke China’s AI chip supply”.

Grand Theft Auto VI: the cultural event of the decade?

This week, after a 13-year wait, gamers will finally get hold of Grand Theft Auto VI, the latest instalment of the most successful console computer game in history. How did a game of stealing cars and shooting strangers become such an enormous cultural phenomenon? The Guardian’s video games editor, Keza MacDonald, traces the history of games by Rockstar, GTA’s creator, and what its most successful product has told us about the US, the setting of all its games so far.

A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

Some travellers seek out ancient landmarks when they visit a new place. Hidde Burgmans, from the Netherlands, looks for ancient trees – and he’s created an app of the same name to help people find remarkable old trees around the world, from Malaysian baobabs to the Fortingall yew in Perthshire, Scotland, thought to be an astounding 5,000 years old.

Users can review remarkable old trees around the world, and upload their favourites to the Ancient Trees app. “On Tuesday somebody photographed a tree in Edinburgh. Today, someone in Freiburg,” said Burgmans. “That just makes me happy. I thought it was quite a niche, geeky thing, but apparently more people are interested in ancient trees than I thought.”

Sign up here for a weekly roundup of The Upside, sent to you every Sunday

And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.

title: UK exposed to polycrisis of threats amid government ‘complacency’
excerpt:
Lords report calls for urgent new approach to resilience planning in face of cyber-attacks, sabotage and climate crisis

Ministers are complacent in the face of fast-changing and increasingly intercon...
body_text:
Lords report calls for urgent new approach to resilience planning in face of cyber-attacks, sabotage and climate crisis

Ministers are complacent in the face of fast-changing and increasingly interconnected threats to the UK, and must act quickly to increase national resilience to possibly very major crises, a parliamentary report has found.

While Labour recently launched a “Be Ready” campaign, advising households to have stocks of food and water, most of the public are unaware of the scale of potential threats from cyber-attacks, proxy acts of violence or strikes on underseas cables, as well as natural disasters such as extreme weather and flooding, it said.

Written by the Lords national resilience committee after months of expert hearings, the report calls for a new and coherent approach to resilience planning, including a dedicated cabinet minister and an annual statement to parliament by the prime minister to set out the extent of preparedness.

It also called for more flexible ways to communicate with the public, including a pause to plans to switch off the Freeview-style digital terrestrial TV signal, in case other systems are disrupted.

Another recommendation is for the government to send every household a booklet setting out how people can prepare for and respond to an emergency, following the model of countries such as Denmark and Sweden.

The report said the UK’s current plans were often out of date and over atomised, dealing with responses to a single emergency such as a loss of power or water supplies, or a cyber-attack, and not an increasingly plausible “polycrisis” of several disruptions blending into another, especially as AI “supercharges” the risk from cyber-attacks.

“In the face of potentially catastrophic risks and despite the recent launch of the Be Ready campaign, the government appears complacent and the UK is underprepared. We need to move fast to turn things around,” the committee warned.

“The government must not treat emerging threats as distant or hypothetical problems. Doing so risks leaving the UK exposed as vulnerabilities develop.”

Among the particular vulnerabilities highlighted are medicines and food, both of which are dependent on highly centralised and generally international supply chains, with few if any back-up options if these are disrupted.

The bulk of antibiotic medicines are now made in China or India, the report noted, with about 90% of the world’s 6-APA, the organic compound which is the basis of penicillin-types antibiotics, coming from China.

This is, it said, the result of years of price pressures and cost-based procurement, meaning there is now only one integrated penicillin facility in Europe, and none in the UK.

The same is true for other medical supplies, with one witness telling the committee that such was the reliance on overseas-made items such as scissors and medical staplers that disrupted could badly disrupt many everyday surgical operations.

With food, the committee was told that while people stockpiling several days of food and water, as recommended by Be Ready, was something, this did not cover the wider strategic risks to a hugely centralised food system.

This results in almost 95% of UK retail food being supplied by just nine companies from 131 distribution hubs, meaning that disruption to just a handful of firms could create very significant disruption.

Despite the increasing risk of multi-area crises, too much current emergency planning remains “organised in silos around individual risks, organisations and sectors, rather than the continued operation of essential national functions”, the report said, calling for this to change.

There was, it set out, a particular risk to digital communications, including through possible attacks on undersea cables. BT, which has a dominant role in this area, has access to just two cable repair ships, the report found – “one French-owned and generally unavailable, and one UK-based but 35 years old”.

Among its recommendations, the report said the Cabinet Office, which leads on resilience, should set out a national resilience strategy within six months, with proper funding and a more coherent assessment than the current national risk register, which lists 87 separate items.

It also called for resilience to be embedded in civilian life, with a national register of volunteers and civil reservists drawn up, and the possibility of an entitlement to paid leave for people taking resilience-based training.

Jean Coussins, the cross-bench peer who chairs the committee, said ministers should not be “squeamish” about setting out the risks.

She said: “Evidence shows that the public would be reassured, not alarmed, by candid information. People are more than willing to step up in an emergency, but less clear [as to] why and how.”

A spokesperson for the Cabinet Office said it would “carefully review” the specific recommendations, but that the government was already working at speed.

“From launching a national campaign to raise awareness of the simple steps households can take to stay safe in everyday emergencies, to delivering the largest home defence exercise in recent history next year, and investing over £1bn in pandemic security – our work on resilience goes further than successive governments have ever gone before.

“However, we know there is still more work to do to make the UK the most resilient country we can be, including working with and learning from our allies.”

title: Home Office accused of trying to cancel online talk by Andreas Malm
excerpt:
Hackney mayor decries ‘assault’ on free speech over event featuring Swedish academic who is banned from entering UK

Shabana Mahmood has been accused of an “assault” on free speech over claims her off...
body_text:
Hackney mayor decries ‘assault’ on free speech over event featuring Swedish academic who is banned from entering UK

Shabana Mahmood has been accused of an “assault” on free speech over claims her officials tried to cancel an online talk by the climate academic Andreas Malm days after he was banned from entering the UK.

The event in Hackney, east London, was a launch party for the socialist magazine Tribune. It went ahead on 4 November in defiance of Home Office warnings.

While the Home Office has denied it tried to cancel the event, its officials warned Hackney council, which owns the venue, that the event could breach counter-terrorism laws because it was also due to be addressed by the Palestine Action cofounder Huda Ammori. The event took place on the day she was challenging the group’s proscription in the supreme court.

Hackney’s Green party mayor, Zoe Garbett, who intervened to ensure the event went ahead, has accused Mahmood of an “appalling assault on free speech” and written to her demanding an explanation.

Days before the event, Malm, a respected Swedish climate academic and author of How to Blow Up a Pipeline, was prevented from travelling to the UK. Officials told him that his presence was “not considered to be conducive to the public good”, but no further reasons were given.

Documents released to Tribune under freedom of information laws detail how Hackney council officials appeared to have been pressed by the Home Office to cancel the event, despite the department’s own assessment that it was “unlikely to meet the threshold for disruption”.

An email on 12 October from the Home Office’s extremism disruptions team said: “We received this referral from the counter-extremism group (CEG) about [Malm] due to visit the UK for an event in London on 4 November.

“[Malm] has made many statements in support of terrorists and direct action, particularly regarding Palestine and climate change.”

After Malm was prevented from entering the UK, in a decision that was widely criticised, Tribune said he would still speak at the event via a video link. A day before the event, a Home Office official emailed Hackney council’s Prevent and hate-crime coordinator to describe Malm and Ammori as “two speakers of concern”.

An official from the Home Office’s Prevent local delivery unit also told the council: “Ultimately, I can’t direct you to cancel the event. This is a decision for the council.”

But they went on to warn that the event could breach the Terrorism Act 2000 “whereby it is an offence if a person … assists in arranging … a meeting which he knows is to be addressed by a person who belongs … to a proscribed organisation”.

Mahmood’s officials also asked Hackney if managers of the venue had been told of their concerns about Malm and Ammori speaking at the event “even if it is to take place virtually”.

After those concerns were passed on, a manager at the venue called Tribune to say the event would have to be cancelled, according to its editor, Oliver Eagleton. This decision was then overruled by the mayor.

In her letter to the home secretary, Garbett said: “Encouraging the cancellation of lawful public events represents an assault on the right to free speech and under no circumstance will I be complicit in it.”

She added: “Despite initial Home Office assessments indicating that the event was ‘unlikely to meet the threshold for disruption’, pressure was applied to council staff to intervene with the operator and cancel the booking.”

The letter asked: “Why was pressure exerted on local council officers to consider cancelling or vetoing speakers, and how does the Home Office reconcile these actions with local authorities’ statutory obligations to uphold free speech and peaceful assembly.”

A Home Office spokesperson said it was “categorically untrue to suggest the Home Office pushed for this event to be cancelled”, pointing out it was a decision for the council, informed by Home Office advice.

Malm said: “The UK’s crackdown on free expression is terrifying. First they ban the books of Sally Rooney. Then they block people like me from entering the country because of our support for Palestine. Now it comes to light that they tried to cancel this magazine launch – just because they feared that the speakers might say something they disagree with. Where will this repression end?”

Ammori said: “By trying to prevent me from being able to speak publicly, the Home Office has further proven the case I was making in the supreme court that same day about the authorities misapplying the law to carry out unlawful arrests and unlawful acts of censorship such as this.

“Home Office officials wrongly advised the council that this entirely lawful political discussion would breach the Terrorism Act simply because I was due to participate. I have never been convicted of any crime, let alone a terrorism offence, but people convicted under the Terrorism Act are not gagged as a result and barred from speaking publicly. The suggestion that my participation in a political discussion could somehow make that discussion unlawful is ludicrous.”

title: US and rivals spar over next UN boss as race lurches towards deadline
excerpt: A tense race to replace outgoing United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres is heading into its final few weeks in advance of a deadline that has never been breached, as global powers spar over...
body_text:
A tense race to replace outgoing United Nations Secretary-General Antonio Guterres is heading into its final few weeks in advance of a deadline that has never been breached, as global powers spar over candidates in an opaque election process.

With eight candidates, secret polls and geopolitical rivalries at play, the choice of the UN’s next chief is still up in the air, even as Guterres must leave office on December 31.

Competing interests from the Americas to the Middle East have complicated the process, raising fears that, for the first time in history, the new year could begin without a leader at the helm of the world’s central diplomatic organisation. The late inclusion of two candidates — Emirati diplomat Lana Nusseibeh and Turkish nominee Feridun Sinirlioglu — has further split the race wide open, with no name so far succeeding in overcoming opposition from all five permanent members of the UN Security Council (UNSC), who hold vetoes.

The protracted contest is part of a “struggle over who will exercise political influence within the UN at a time when multilateralism is under considerable pressure and attack”, Georgina Holmes, senior lecturer in politics and international studies at the Open University, United Kingdom, told Al Jazeera.

“P5 member states are not as politically aligned as they have been in previous eras, arguably even during the Cold War,” said Holmes, referring to the permanent members of the UNSC.

The UN secretary-general has often been compared with a “secular pope” – a figure expected to unite countries and spearhead global diplomacy.

But the position is more than that of a figurehead. The secretary-general is also the UN’s top administrative official, responsible for tapping senior officials and supervising the UN Secretariat’s tens of thousands of staff.

“The secretary-general must be a skilled politician to navigate the geopolitics; a skilled diplomat and mediator to help settle disputes; a charismatic person in the public eye; and a solid and skilled administrator,” Jan Klabbers, professor of international law at the University of Cambridge, told Al Jazeera. “It has been called ‘the most difficult job in the world’ for a reason.”

This year’s race comes as the UN, under Guterres, is under heavy strain, having been sidelined from conflicts in Iran and Ukraine. It has faced blistering criticism from United States President Donald Trump and is suffering a financial crisis that has forced it to let go of thousands of staff.

It also comes as wider geopolitical rivalries extend to the pool of candidates to lead the organisation, who are being scrutinised over their nationalities and policy commitments.

Eight individuals who have been appointed by UN member states are currently in the running to replace Guterres. Most of them are from Latin America or the Caribbean, which is in line with representation according to informal UN protocol. Five of the eight are women, amid a push for the UN to select its first female secretary-general.

A leading contender, according to a series of anonymous straw polls the UNSC carries out to gauge support, is Costa Rican diplomat Rebeca Grynspan.

In the last poll on November 5, which does not show which UNSC members voted which way, Grynspan received 12 “encourage” votes and three “discourage” votes, according to PassBlue, a nonprofit that reports on UN affairs.

Grynspan, who heads the UN Conference on Trade and Development (UNCTAD), has been described as a “continuity candidate”, but there are concerns as to whether she would bring enough reform to an organisation facing huge political and financial pressures.

Richard Gowan, programme director of global issues and institutions at the International Crisis Group, told Al Jazeera that Grynspan had “solidified her position as the frontrunner”, but still appears to face opposition from the US and Russia, which could veto her bid.

While she has avoided directly confronting any veto-wielding nation, some of her reports as UNCTAD head have voiced concerns over Israel’s actions in Gaza and the occupied West Bank, positions at odds with Washington’s more full-throated support for Israel. Grynspan has previously also disagreed with Russian justifications for suspending a deal to allow the transport of grain through the Black Sea.

At the same time, she — like other candidates — is believed to be lobbying with key member states to win their support. In April, she met Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov over her candidature.

“Grynspan’s team argue that they can still nudge Washington and Moscow to accept her, and US officials do seem to be leaving open the possibility of working with her in the end,” said Gowan.

To be elected, a candidate needs at least nine votes in favour in the 15-member UNSC, while avoiding any vetoes from its five permanent members – the US, the UK, France, Russia and China. The 193-member UN General Assembly (UNGA) then ultimately has to sign off.

Ben Donaldson, adviser to the 1 for 8 Billion campaign, a civil society campaign “advocating for a fair, open, inclusive way to select the next secretary-general”, stressed that opposition from P5 members in a straw poll does not necessarily equate to an eventual veto.

“It has been used in the past as a basis to extract a concession from a candidate, very often in the form of a backroom deal to get a P5 national appointed to a key role in the future UN boss’s cabinet,” he told Al Jazeera.

The Argentinian head of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), Rafael Grossi, is also in the running. He finished second in the latest straw poll, with nine “encourage” and four “discourage” votes. However, his reputation for being closely aligned with Washington is expected to hurt him with some P5 members, especially China and Russia, though he has also had warm words for Beijing and Moscow in recent weeks.

The other candidates from Latin America or the Caribbean are Guyanese diplomat Carolyn Rodrigues Birkett, Antigua and Barbuda diplomat Maria Fernanda Espinosa and Ecuadorian diplomat Ivonne A-Baki.

Rodrigues Birkett, whose description of Israel’s actions in Gaza as “genocide” has drawn scrutiny in the US, received five “discourage” votes in the latest straw poll. Espinosa and A-Baki received 10 and 14 “discourage” votes, respectively, making their candidacies unlikely.

The UAE’s Lana Nusseibeh and Turkiye’s Feridun Sinirlioglu, nominated by their countries in recent weeks, have also shaken up the race but face significant opposition.

Nusseibeh is reportedly favoured by the US and Russia, but her candidacy has received pushback over her country’s alleged arming of paramilitary forces accused of atrocities in Sudan. The United Arab Emirates has denied the allegation. Nusseibeh received six “discourage” votes in the latest straw poll.

“Nusseibeh’s main challenge is to win over China, which has so far seemed sceptical about her candidacy,” said Gowan. “If she can get Beijing’s support, she could break through.”

Sinirlioglu’s candidature, which UNSC member Greece is expected to oppose, received eight “discourage” votes.

Ugandan politician Olara Otunnu, the only remaining African candidate, received nine “discourage” votes.

Far-right former Hungarian Prime Minister Viktor Orban, though not an official candidate, has also been floated by the US as an outside choice, The Wall Street Journal has reported.

Several analysts told Al Jazeera that Grynspan appears to be in the best position, though the influence of P5 countries could change the race.

Earlier this month, the US and Russia put their weight behind the UAE’s Nusseibeh, with France and the UK offering “little resistance”, according to diplomats cited by media platform Devex.

China, for its part, has signalled a preference for a Latin American candidate, reports The New York Times, although Beijing has not publicly endorsed anyone.

Ellen Ravndal, associate professor in political science at the University of Stavanger, Norway, told Al Jazeera the drawn-out selection process and struggle to reach consensus reflect an era of “more geopolitical tensions” and a UN that is in “near-constant crisis mode”.

Adam Day, head of the Geneva office of the United Nations University Centre for Policy Research, pointed out that while the leadership contest has been lengthier and more contested than in the previous cycles in which former Secretaries-General Guterres in 2016 and Ban Ki-moon in 2006 were elected, some earlier races stretched into December.

“In the broader scope of secretary-general races, this one is still within the range of what has been normal,” Day told Al Jazeera. “But the longer it takes, the less time the incoming secretary-general has to prepare a transition.”

If no successor to Guterres is selected by the end of the year, the UN Charter does not specify an automatic interim successor. Any gap in the post would therefore require the UNSC and other UN bodies to agree on how to manage organisational leadership and operations.

“There is widespread concern that the United States and possibly other influential states are running down the clock, potentially to increase pressure to settle for a less popular candidate or to leave the UN leaderless and weakened for a period,” said Donaldson.

title: Widow of Haiti’s slain leader Moise to contest presidential vote
excerpt:
The widow of Haiti’s slain President Jovenel Moise, whose 2021 ⁠assassination was ⁠a major turning point for the nation, has registered as a candidate for the first presidential election in a decade.
...
body_text:
The widow of Haiti’s slain President Jovenel Moise, whose 2021 ⁠assassination was ⁠a major turning point for the nation, has registered as a candidate for the first presidential election in a decade.

Martine Moise’s name appeared on the website of the Provisional Electoral Council (CEP) as a candidate ⁠on Sunday.

A ⁠first-round vote is set for July next year.

Haiti last held a presidential election in 2016. Successive leaders have repeatedly delayed elections, citing insecurity risks, amid the expanding influence of powerful and heavily armed gangs.

“Haiti will rise again on its own two feet, because politics needs to be done differently,” Moise, who has not publicly commented on the registration, said on X last week.

In the post, she also blamed “the opposition” for bringing the country “to its knees”. “They do not want the country to develop; they do not want the people to live well,” she said.

Martine Moise is one of three ‌women among 33 registered presidential candidates. Among other prominent candidates are Michel Martelly and Jocelerme Privert, both former presidents, former Prime Minister Claude Joseph and former Foreign Minister Dominique Dupuy.

Several candidates, including Martelly and Privert, have been sanctioned internationally over accusations, which they both deny, of supporting armed gangs.

Martine Moise has been a key witness in the Miami court case prosecuting dozens of suspects involved in the murder of her husband, who led ⁠Haiti from 2017 until his death in July 2021.

He ⁠was shot in his bedroom by Colombian mercenaries impersonating agents of the United States Drug Enforcement Administration. Martine Moise suffered serious gunshot wounds and was flown to a hospital in Florida.

A series of transitional governments followed, as armed gangs, widely believed to be aided by corrupt politicians, seized control of ⁠much of the capital, Port-au-Prince, and surrounding regions.

About 1.5 million people have been displaced and more than 22,000 have been killed, many by security personnel. Several international forces have been deployed to Haiti to help police fight the gangs; the most recent deployment, last month, involved soldiers from El Salvador.

Last week, Haitian security forces regained control of the country’s main stadium, which had been under gang control for two years, forcing the national football team to play elsewhere.

The operation was part of a deployment of about 2,000 soldiers ordered by El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele, who announced that the troops would set up an operational base in the stadium to push further into territory still controlled by the gangs.
