title: Wife of assassinated ex-Haitian leader registers for presidential election
excerpt:
Martine Moise was injured in the gun attack that killed her husband

The widow of assassinated former Haitian president Jovenel Moise has registered as a presidential candidate for next year's electio...
body_text:
Martine Moise was injured in the gun attack that killed her husband

The widow of assassinated former Haitian president Jovenel Moise has registered as a presidential candidate for next year's elections in the Caribbean nation.

Martine Moise was injured in the gun attack that killed her husband at their home in the capital, Port-au-Prince, in 2021.

Haiti, which last held an election in 2016, has been plagued with chronic instability and gang violence.

Elections were scheduled to be held in December but were postponed last month until July due to the country's insecurity.

Moise has to comment on her candidacy but the electoral council website showed her registration on Sunday.

Last week she said on X:  "Haiti will rise again on its own two feet, because politics needs to be done differently."

A total of 33 candidates have registered for the elections, including former presidents Michel Martelly and Jocelerme Privert, former prime minister Claude Joseph and former foreign minister Dominique Dupuy.

Jovenel Moise, who led Haiti from 2017 until his death, was shot dead at his home in Port-au-Prince in July 2021, allegedly by a group of mainly Colombian mercenaries.

Martine Moise suffered serious gunshot wounds during the attack and was flown to a hospital in Florida.

She was charged in connection with the assassination in 2024, but the indictment was overturned last year.

The assassination shook the Caribbean nation to its core, with many Haitians shocked that the 53-year-old was killed with such apparent ease.

Thirty suspects have been indicted over the killing so far and in September 18 people were flown from Haiti to Florida to stand trial for their alleged involvement in the assassination.

Haiti has been engulfed in a wave of gang violence since the assassination of Moise.

At least 1,408 people were killed and 656 injured from April through to June this year, according to the UN Integrated Office in Haiti.

title: MP Helen Haines’s first words since leaving hospital after alleged attack led to double amputation
excerpt:
Independent MP says she is ‘overwhelmed’ by thousands of warm wishes and thanks Australians for charity donations

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

The independent Austra...
body_text:
Independent MP says she is ‘overwhelmed’ by thousands of warm wishes and thanks Australians for charity donations

Get our daily political email, free app or daily news podcast

The independent Australian MP Helen Haines has been discharged from hospital, four weeks after she was allegedly attacked by a man outside her electorate office in Victoria resulting in the amputation of both her legs.

In a statement, Haines said she had moved to the rehabilitation stage of her recovery, which would continue in Melbourne.

“This is a really positive moment, and I am full of gratitude for the expert and compassionate care I received at the Alfred [hospital] and am receiving in this next stage,” Haines said.

“I appreciate the thousands of warm wishes and supportive messages from people across Indi, throughout Australia and around the world. They are giving me strength as I focus on this next phase of healing.”

The prime minister, Anthony Albanese, said his thoughts were with Haines.

“We continue to provide support to Helen, her family, community and staff as she undertakes her rehabilitation,” Albanese said in a statement.

Haines said she was “overwhelmed” by the many Australians who had donated to the Save the Children charity fundraiser.

Her husband, Phil Haines, had made the request to the public on her behalf to donate to the charity in lieu of flowers in the aftermath of the alleged attack.

As of Monday afternoon, more than $1.46m had been raised for the charity through Haines’s fundraising appeal.

“I am overwhelmed by the generosity of Australians in the form of donations to Save the Children and I look forward to working with them in due course on applying these funds to improve the lives of children.”

Haines, the federal member for the Victorian seat of Indi, had been in a critical but stable condition after she was repeatedly struck by a vehicle in Wangaratta on 19 October. Her condition was then downgraded to “serious but stable” on 24 October.

Police will allege the 65-year-old was standing by the boot of her car outside her electoral office when a car did a U-turn and struck her repeatedly.

Tarrawingee man Brendan Nugent, 43, has been charged and the incident continues to be investigated. He is known to her family.

Police charged Nugent with dangerous driving causing serious injury, intentionally cause serious injury and the commonwealth offence of causing harm to a commonwealth public official.

Police have also charged him with two additional offences – cultivating and possessing cannabis – according to court documents.

The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, paid tribute to Haines in the Senate on Monday and on behalf of the parliament wished her strength through her challenging rehabilitation.

“It says a great deal about her character that even as she faces these challenges, in her statement she looks ahead to the work she wants to do to improve the lives of children following the donations to Save the Children that Australians made at her request. It is an example of her determination and her generosity that is so admired,” Wong said.

The leader of the opposition in the Senate, Michaelia Cash, added that Haines’s discharge from hospital was warmly welcomed across the parliament.

“She has demonstrated extraordinary courage and resilience. And on behalf, in particular, of my Coalition Senate colleagues, we wish Helen every strength during her continued recovery.”

Haines has been given leave of absence until 26 November, the last sitting day of the year.

MPs across parliament have expressed concern for their safety and that of their staff since the alleged attack, and prompted conversations about the temperature of political debate.

Albanese, during the last parliamentary sitting, warned against the rise in anger “that distorts and corrodes our public discourse”, and urged voters and politicians not to ignore it.

“Enabled by the anonymity and speed afforded by social media, we are seeing rage and aggression increasing, not just in politics, but towards workers in hospitality and retail, in schools and in hospitals, towards police, paramedics, and other officials, we are seeing a normalisation of the language of grievance and violence.”

The independent MP Allegra Spender said it was “wonderful” news that Haines was making good progress in her recovery.

“She is a remarkable person and her strength and positivity after everything that has happened inspires me.”

title: Megaspeed, the company linked to the downfall of Nvidia boss, says it’s a ‘legitimate and lawful business’
excerpt:
Company insists Alice Huang, accused of being a Chinese spy, left business in late 2025

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Megaspeed International, the company linked to the...
body_text:
Company insists Alice Huang, accused of being a Chinese spy, left business in late 2025

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Megaspeed International, the company linked to the downfall of the Nvidia chief, Jensen Huang, says it is a “legitimate and lawful business” and has announced that its director, who allegedly had an affair with Huang, left the business in late 2025.

The Singapore-based cloud computing company on the weekend said it was “aware of recent media reports containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence”.

Megaspeed said it had “retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation”.

Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the chip manufacturer Nvidia after reports of extramarital affairs with Alice Huang and two company employees.

US intelligence agencies believe the tech chief, whose products have been crucial to the AI boom, had been targeted by Alice Huang, the former director of Megaspeed International.

US officials have alleged Alice Huang may have been acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times has reported.

Megaspeed in the past three years has been one of Nvidia’s biggest foreign customers, purchasing nearly $5bn in AI chips and advanced hardware. A US senator asked the commerce department to investigate whether Megaspeed had diverted Nvidia chips to China.

Megaspeed said on Sunday it would not comment on Alice Huang’s “personal and private matters”.

“Alice Huang officially left Megaspeed effective August 30, 2025 and currently has no role with the company,” it’s statement read.

The global facades of Megaspeed International form a puzzling corporate picture, and involve a lottery retailer in rural Australia, a dilapidated storefront in Kuala Lumpur and a near-empty office in Singapore.

The company on Sunday said: “Megaspeed designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate.”

Short seller Culper Research in May this year quoted a Megaspeed employee as saying Alice Huang was “still our boss”, in a report accusing Nvidia of having a “China problem”.

On Thursday, Singaporean authorities said Huang had been barred from re-entering the city state after a 2025 investigation into the company’s “suspected breaches of our domestic laws”.

The ministry of home affairs said it had held Alice Huang’s passport from June 2025 until February. Police believed she had given them “inaccurate” information, to downplay her role at the company, but released her due to insufficient evidence.

She was issued a stern warning and barred from re-entering the country. Taiwan has also barred her from re-entry, its authorities have said.

Singapore’s initial investigation related to Megaspeed’s potential “false declarations” over the purchase of computer servers.

On Friday, Malaysia said it was investigating a subsidiary of Megaspeed International over the possible diversion of advanced AI chips to other countries.

Megaspeed has previously said there was no evidence of illegal chip transfers.

Its registered Sydney office is home to numerous business and had no Megaspeed signage, mailbox or physical presence when the Guardian visited last week. No one had heard of Megaspeed Australia or its listed director, 29-year-old Kai Kang.

Reuters visited a news agency and lottery retailer, in Seymour, Victoria, an hour’s drive north of Melbourne, where a woman, who identified herself as Kang’s mother, said Kang was based in Shanghai and did not know anything about the Singaporean company.

Kang has not been accused of any wrongdoing. Attempts to contact him were unsuccessful.

The US attorney general, Todd Blanche, said last week that the Justice Department had not concluded whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy. Asked whether she was a spy, the president, Donald Trump, said: “I don’t know if that’s been determined yet.”

Beijing rejected the allegations as unsubstantiated. Associated Press was unable to reach Alice Huang for comment. The Guardian was seeking comment from Huang.

Megaspeed began as the overseas arm of a Chinese video game developer and was incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International. It adopted its current name in March 2023, when all its shares were transferred to Huang Le Limited, a British Virgin Islands company. Alice Huang is also known by her Chinese name, Huang Le.

By November 2023, she was no longer listed as a Megaspeed director, and all her shares had been transferred to an entity owned by Singaporean businessman Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan.

The company’s finances have also attracted attention. Singapore corporate records show its total assets rose roughly 90-fold from end-2023 to 2024, reaching almost $3bn.

title: ‘The blood of these brothers cries out’: Pope Leo demands justice for people killed protecting the Amazon
excerpt:
Pontiff delivers forceful speech on final day in Peru as he travels from high in the Andes into the Amazon

Pope Leo XIV has demanded justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting the Amaz...
body_text:
Pontiff delivers forceful speech on final day in Peru as he travels from high in the Andes into the Amazon

Pope Leo XIV has demanded justice for environmental defenders killed for protecting the Amazon and backed efforts by Indigenous peoples to stop their lands from being ravaged by logging and illegal mining.

On the penultimate day of his South American tour, Leo on Sunday travelled into the Peruvian Amazon and channelled one of Pope Francis’s core teachings that links care for the most vulnerable with care for God’s creation.

“The cry of the Earth and the cry of the poor are inseparable,” Leo told Indigenous representatives and missionaries gathered along the Ucayali River in the north-eastern city of Pucallpa.

He said he came to Pucallpa to support them in their search for justice and peace and referred to what environmental groups estimate have been 57 murders of environmental defenders between 2010 and 2024.

“The blood of these brothers cries out to God and demands justice,” Leo said to applause from the crowd, many of whom were wearing traditional feathered headwear and face markings of the region.

In addition to deforestation, illegal gold mining has become an increasingly lucrative business in the Amazon, devastating forests and polluting rivers. Illegal mining and coca production has also driven deforestation.

Leo addressed the combination of threats in one of his most forceful speeches to date, drawing on his years of experience as a Peruvian bishop and Francis’s constant preaching about the environment and the plight of Indigenous groups.

During the encounter and a subsequent mass in Pucallpa, he demanded a different model of economic development that respects the Earth and the Indigenous peoples who care for it, rather than the “irresponsible exploitation” by outside actors.

“Very little has been done – and very slowly at that – while the means to exploit and pollute creation have accelerated,” he said at mass. “In the face of these evils, let us not bury the Lord’s gifts, for he gives us the strength to repair and heal the suffering caused by an insatiable thirst for domination.”

In Peru, most murders of environmental defenders go unpunished; only a few have resulted in convictions.

The most recent conviction came in the case of Kichwa leader Quinto Inuma Alvarado, who was murdered in 2023 when he was ambushed by hitmen on a river in the San Martín region, the Amazonian territory he was defending.

Leo also referred to a notorious rise in sexual violence against Indigenous Awajún and Wampis schoolgirls in the northern Amazon, and blasted the “impunity” and “corruption” surrounding them.

The Awajún and Wampis Women’s Council has recorded 370 cases of sexual violence in the Condorcanqui province between January and July.

Leo’s last full day in Peru was also his most ambitious, crisscrossing the nation to minister to communities high in the Andes mountains. Peru’s air force released footage of the pope inside a helicopter and said it was “an unforgettable memory” to take Leo around the country.

His first stop was the mountain city of Cusco, where huge crowds greeted him.

“It is all worth it,” said Margarida Salomon, 63, who said she came from Sucre in Bolivia to see the pontiff, spending about $500 to take a bus and sleep in a tent. “I am still getting to know this pope, but the fact he is here in the Andes means a lot.”

The visit to Cusco, 3,400m (more than 11,000ft) above sea level, tested Leo’s stamina as he continues recovering from lung cancer surgery last month. Leo sat in the chair of his popemobile during part of the ride around Cusco, but it wasn’t clear if that was to preserve his energy or to steady himself on the uneven streets.

In general, the 71-year-old Leo has seemed unfazed by the toll of the three-nation South American trip, the longest of his pontificate.

title: Russell Brand’s wife opens up after comedian’s rape conviction, shares message from imprisoned husband
excerpt:
Fox News senior foreign affairs correspondent Greg Palkot reports on Russell Brand's sentencing following his convictions for rape and sexual assault in London.

Russell Brand's wife, Laura Brand, bro...
body_text:
Fox News senior foreign affairs correspondent Greg Palkot reports on Russell Brand's sentencing following his convictions for rape and sexual assault in London.

Russell Brand's wife, Laura Brand, broke her silence Sunday, nearly one week after the actor was convicted of rape and sexual assault and sentenced to more than 10 years in prison.

Laura, 39, appeared alone to present the couple's weekly Sunday Service Youtube vlog, which she admitted would look "a little different this week" after his conviction.

"I’m here without Russell, but we’ve decided to keep going," Laura shared of the sermon which was partially recorded during the trial.

BEAR GRYLLS ADDRESSES RUSSELL BRAND'S BAPTISM, CALLS VICTIMS 'HEROES OF THE DAY' AFTER VERDICT

Russell Brand was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison last week after being convicted of rape. (James Manning)

"I open with a reading from Philippians, then share an episode we recorded together during the trial that we’d been holding back. We talk about why some of the coverage sounds like a football match and what it’s like to pray when something has taken over your whole week. I read some of your comments, share a little Brother Lawrence and close with a message Russell asked me to read. Thank you for being here with me."

RUSSELL BRAND FOUND GUILTY OF ONE COUNT OF RAPE AND THREE COUNTS OF SEXUAL ASSAULT

While sitting in front of a window, Laura began the weekly series with the intention to "continue the good work that was being established here in this Sunday service community."

"It may look different, but the ambitions are very much the same and we trust God and we trust his plan, and we trust everything he's doing right now," she said.

Russell Brand was found guilty last week of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault following a four-week criminal trial. (Elizabeth Cook/PA Wire via Zuma Press)

Laura Brand appeared in court to support her husband. (Getty Images)

"Even though it's painful and obviously will take some getting used to for me to even sit here and not have my companion and my person with me ... I want to continue and I'm grateful for the support, and I'm grateful for you and thank you for your messages."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Laura noted that while Russell was not with her at the moment, she said that "the Holy Spirit is moving, and the Holy Spirit cannot be restrained."

"I'm speaking to Russell. He's OK and he's praying," Laura said. "Unsurprisingly, he's praying and we decided for me to continue. He asked if I would read the rest of the Philippians passage, which I will continue to do now, from his Bible."

She then said she had a note from Russell, and read it out loud: "Beloved brothers and sisters in Christ, God bless you for your support. As you know, I am not guilty for the offenses I have been jailed for, so something strange is happening."

Laura continued: "The good news is that Christ is with us when we choose him, and I do. I am incarcerated in HMP Littlehey. Little as in small, and hey as in, ‘Hey, I’m in the biggest sex offenders’ prison in Europe. The good news is that I have already seen that the staff here are strong, they are kind, and they are dedicated. And as for my fellow prisoners, I now know that I am in no position to judge anyone."

"I don’t know which other men here are not guilty, and the ones that are, they are people that Christ died to save, like you and me. Let us all love, pray for, and forgive one another as God forgave us."

"Please support my treasured wife and family. I feel your prayers, your brother in Christ. Russell," she concluded the note.

On Nov. 5, a London jury found Brand, 51, guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault involving four women, stemming from incidents between 2004-09.

Laura Brand mouthed ‘I love you’ to her husband, Russell Brand, after being sentenced to more than 10 years in prison on rape charges. (Priscilla Coleman/MB Media)

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

He denied the charges and was acquitted of two additional rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Brand was immediately taken into custody following the verdict, according to the BBC. Upon release, the comedian will also be required to register as a sex offender for life.

During sentencing on Monday, Mr. Justice Joel Bennathan said Brand had demonstrated a "casual and arrogant disregard" for women’s right to refuse his sexual advances.

Russell Brand was immediately taken into custody following the verdict. (Elizabeth Cook/PA via AP)

"About 20 years ago, Russell Brand, you were becoming famous," Bennathan said. "You were clever — and in many people’s eyes, funny and charismatic. You had also become a sexual predator."

The judge described one of Brand’s sexual assaults as "outrageous and possibly laddish, but also a criminal offense," adding that Brand’s behavior reflected his belief that "fame meant you could act how you liked, when you liked, unhindered by the rules by which decent people live."

WATCH: RUSSELL BRAND POLICE INTERVIEW FOOTAGE RELEASED AFTER RAPE CONVICTION

According to Sky News, as Brand was taken from the dock by three guards, he turned to his wife and nodded, saying, "We'll be OK."

Laura reportedly mouthed back: "I love you, I'll be OK."

The couple has been married since 2017 and share three children together.

title: Seahawks receiver Tory Horton made one of the smartest plays you'll ever see in Seattle's win over Las Vegas
excerpt:
Baltimore Ravens star Kyle Hamilton tells OutKick that the team has gotten "unlucky" but still has the capability to win games.

Seattle Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald is a Super Bowl champion for...
body_text:
Baltimore Ravens star Kyle Hamilton tells OutKick that the team has gotten "unlucky" but still has the capability to win games.

Seattle Seahawks head coach Mike Macdonald is a Super Bowl champion for a reason. He's a damn good football coach. Perhaps nothing showed how well Seattle is coached quite like a play Seahawks receiver Tory Horton made in the final minutes.

With the Seahawks leading 21-10, Matt Gay kicked a 43-yard field goal to make it a one-score game. The Raiders had 2:04 on the clock and two timeouts left as they lined up for the ensuing kickoff, leaving them with a decision. They could attempt an onside kick or just kick it deep and play defense.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Las Vegas elected to kick it deep, but that brought another problem into play. If the Seahawks could burn at least four seconds off the clock during the kick return, it would take the game to the two-minute warning and eliminate one of the remaining clock stoppages.

Seattle Seahawks receiver Tory Horton made one of the smartest football plays I've ever seen. (Getty Images)

So, the Raiders had two choices: kick the ball out of the back of the end zone or deliberately kick the ball out of bounds along the sideline. If the Raiders weren’t sure Gay could get it out the back, I think they should’ve kicked it out of bounds and lived with giving Seattle the ball at the 40. A touchback would’ve put Seattle at the 35.

Gay elected the former and booted the ball as far as he could. His kick sailed into the air and appeared headed out of the end zone. But that's when Horton made one of the smartest football plays I think I've ever seen.

HIGH SCHOOL FOOTBALL GAME ENDS WITH THREE LATERALS, A FOOLED DEFENSE & THE HIGHEST IQ PLAY YOU'LL EVER SEE

The Seahawks wide receiver leapt and swatted the kick before it could sail out the back of the end zone. Once the ball hit the ground, Horton immediately started pointing at teammate Rashid Shaheed, as if to say, "pick it up and run!"

Tory Horton's heads-up play allowed the Seattle Seahawks to run five crucial seconds off the clock against the Raiders. (Getty Images)

Shaheed did exactly that, scooping up the ball in the end zone and returning it to the Seahawks’ 19-yard line. But, more importantly, he ran five seconds off the clock and brought the game to the two-minute warning. Macdonald came onto the field with a huge smile, celebrating and congratulating Horton for making the heads-up play.

After the play, officials huddled and spoke with Raiders head coach Klint Kubiak. According to the official gamebook, they flagged Horton for an illegal bat, and Las Vegas declined the penalty.

CBS rules analyst Gene Steratore said he didn’t think Horton’s play was illegal. The rulebook backs him up. Rule 12-5-1(b) prohibits batting a loose ball in the end zone after it has touched the ground. Horton swatted the kick before it ever hit the turf.

Seattle Seahawks head coach Mike MacDonald was pumped up after Tory Horton's heads-up play. (Getty Images)

Seattle took over at its own 19 with 1:59 left. If Las Vegas had used both remaining timeouts on the first two downs and then stopped Seattle inbounds on third down, the Seahawks could have burned up to 40 seconds before punting. Drew Lock made that moot when he ran for 15 yards on second-and-11. He took three knees from there to finish off a 21-13 win.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Although it didn't end up mattering, Tory Horton deserves a ton of credit for one of the smartest plays I've ever seen a football player make.

And Seahawks special teams coordinator Jay Harbaugh probably deserves a raise, too.

title: Elon Musk joins 158,000 others calling for Nvidia to bring back Jensen Huang in open letter
excerpt:
Silicon Valley figures back CEO ousted after revelations of affair with suspected Chinese spy, as US treasury secretary urges Nvidia to carry out ‘dramatic shake-up’

Elon Musk and a host of other tec...
body_text:
Silicon Valley figures back CEO ousted after revelations of affair with suspected Chinese spy, as US treasury secretary urges Nvidia to carry out ‘dramatic shake-up’

Elon Musk and a host of other tech executives are among more than 158,000 signatories of an open letter calling for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement as Nvidia chief, days after he resigned from the multi-trillion dollar chip company.

The letter demands that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts”.

Huang’s resignation on Thursday ended a 33-year run at the helm of the AI giant he co-founded, after revelations he had at least two extramarital affairs, one with a woman accused of spying for China and another with a subordinate.

US lawmakers from both sides of the aisle have demanded Huang and Nvidia appear before Congress to explain whether US national security had been put at risk – with some in the president’s own party suggesting that Donald Trump’s administration must also must answer questions on what it knew about Huang’s relationship with the suspected Chinese spy.

According to the Financial Times, Huang has discussed a possible return to the company with people close to him. One Huang ally told the paper they were putting together ⁠a “war room” of Silicon Valley executives to lobby ​for the former Nvidia ‌chief’s return ‌and would try to garner support from ‌the White House.

“Everyone that matters in tech outside the frontier labs loves Jensen,” the person said, adding that the efforts had Huang’s support.

On Friday, two major shareholders, investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker, urged the board to keep “all options” open.

In Washington, however, US treasury secretary Scott Bessent argued on Sunday that Nvidia should look “outside” the company for its next chief. “They need a dramatic shake-up,” Bessent said on Fox News.

Bessent also called on Nvidia to explain whether it knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach China, saying this was more important than Huang’s affair with the alleged spy for Beijing.

The US forbids sales to China of the most cutting-edge AI chips, as parts of its strategy to stay ahead of Beijing in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.

In late 2025, Trump authorised sales of Nvidia chips called H200s to the Chinese – but not the most advanced chips used to run AI models reshaping modern society.

“Nothing above the H200s can be sold to the Chinese,” Bessent said, adding that it was important to examine “whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the US export restrictions”.

Bessent said he wanted answers from Nvidia and its internal investigation of Jensen Huang’s behaviour within the next 10 days.

Alongside Musk, the tech heavyweight signatories on the letter calling for Huang’s return include Tim Sweeney, founder and CEO of video game publisher Epic Games, and Garry Tan, president of Y Combinator, San Francisco’s most renowned business incubator.

Another signatory, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, wrote that Huang had “erred, yes – to err is to be human – but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company”.

More than 7,500 signatories identified themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to 18% of the company’s workforce.

The support illustrates the unique standing of Huang, who is seen as a godfather of AI within the industry. Under his leadership, Nvidia became a pivotal Silicon Valley investor, financing datacentres and startups, earning it the nickname “the central bank of AI”.

But the company has also faced criticism that it has fuelled a speculative investment bubble. Huang fought any constraints on the AI race, clashing on these issues with Claude creator Anthropic and its chief Dario Amodei.

Jensen Huang and other Nvidia officials have agreed to testify before Congress, according to officials, but no date has been set yet.

title: Huge waves pummel California coast, forcing closure of popular piers
excerpt:
Large waves up to 50ft flooded southern California streets and prompted evacuation warning near coastal city

The California coast was pummeled again on Sunday by huge waves that inundated beaches, fl...
body_text:
Large waves up to 50ft flooded southern California streets and prompted evacuation warning near coastal city

The California coast was pummeled again on Sunday by huge waves that inundated beaches, flooded local streets and forced the closure of popular piers.

The National Weather Service office for the San Francisco Bay Area warned that surf up to 35ft (11 meters) was possible, along with dangerous rip currents and sneaker waves.

“Stay out of the water, stay off rocks and jetties, and never turn your back on the ocean!” the weather service said on social media.

On Saturday, waves above 50ft were recorded in San Mateo county, just south of San Francisco.

Surfers weren’t deterred, taking advantage of giant waves at the famous Mavericks beach near Half Moon Bay.

Farther south, the Santa Cruz county sheriff’s office issued an evacuation warning near the coastal town of Capitola that took the brunt of the powerful surf.

In southern California, several piers, including ones in Ventura, Manhattan Beach, Huntington Beach and San Diego’s Pacific Beach, were closed during the weekend as they were slammed by waves.

At La Jolla Cove near San Diego, known for its lounging sea lions, water overflowed the beach and crashed up a staircase leading to the sand.

Conditions were calming by Sunday afternoon, but large waves were expected all week, forecasters warned.

The ongoing super El Niño has warmed the ocean, leading to an increased volume of seawater.

title: Founder of Guadalajara cartel dies in hospital after decades in prison
excerpt:
Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo, the founder of one of Mexico’s first major drug cartels, has died in hospital at age 80.

Local security authorities said Felix Gallardo was transferred to a private hospi...
body_text:
Miguel Angel Felix Gallardo, the founder of one of Mexico’s first major drug cartels, has died in hospital at age 80.

Local security authorities said Felix Gallardo was transferred to a private hospital in the western city of Guadalajara two days ago but suffered multiple organ failure and died at about 2pm (20:00 GMT) on Sunday.

Felix Gallardo, a founder of the Guadalajara cartel, was convicted for the 1985 killing of a US drug-enforcement agent, a crime that made him one of the country’s most notorious traffickers.

Imprisoned since 1989, Felix Gallardo was held in a maximum-security prison in western Jalisco state, though his lawyers repeatedly sought house arrest on the grounds of his deteriorating health.

Rising to prominence in the 1970s, the former cartel kingpin was an architect of Mexico’s modern drug-trafficking trade, igniting a series of turf wars that have led to hundreds of thousands of deaths and disappearances in the ensuing decades.

Born in 1946 in Culiacan, Sinaloa, a northwestern state that would later become synonymous with narco-trafficking, he worked as a police officer and a bodyguard for a local governor. Later, he gained a reputation as a powerful criminal capo known as the “boss of bosses”.

Felix Gallardo and others set up their cartel in Guadalajara, the Jalisco state capital and a fast-growing economic powerhouse, becoming the first to move cocaine to the US on a massive scale and to forge an alliance with Colombian drug barons, including Pablo Escobar’s Medellin cartel.

His narcotics empire expanded in the 1970s and 1980s thanks to bribes that won protection from corrupt officials. His cartel also made innovations, such as using light aircraft to move drugs across the continent, supported by fellow kingpins like Rafael Caro Quintero.

His legal battles stretched across decades. Arrested in 1989, Felix Gallardo was sentenced to 40 years in prison on drug trafficking and weapons charges tied to the Guadalajara cartel.

While already jailed, he faced a separate prosecution over the 1985 kidnapping and murder of US Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) agent Enrique “Kiki” Camarena and Mexican pilot Alfredo Zavala Avelar.

Camarena’s killing caused a diplomatic dispute with Washington, which pressured Mexico to arrest those involved.

In 2017, a federal court found Felix Gallardo guilty in the case and imposed a further 37-year sentence. He denied responsibility for the killings.

His rise and fall were portrayed on screen by Mexican actor Diego Luna in the 2018 hit Netflix series Narcos: Mexico.

Felix Gallardo suffered poor health in his final years and was blind in one eye, practically deaf, and unable to walk on his own by the time Spanish-language US network Telemundo interviewed him in prison in 2021. He maintained his innocence.

“Thirty-two years have passed,” he said. “That’s an eternity for a man who did not commit any crime.”

title: After a nationwide ground stop, US faces aviation infrastructure questions
excerpt:
Last Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) grounded all flights in the United States for nearly four hours due to a reported equipment failure.

It was only the second time since the attac...
body_text:
Last Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) grounded all flights in the United States for nearly four hours due to a reported equipment failure.

It was only the second time since the attacks on September 11, 2001, that such an order was given.

More than 9,000 flights were cancelled, and an estimated 1.5 million passengers were left stranded.

Officials blamed the disruptions on an upgrade gone awry. The routers used to communicate with aeroplanes in mid-flight had suddenly stopped working, and pilots were no longer able to speak on their usual frequencies.

As of Sunday, officials were still working to return the system to normal. “As we look to the end of the day and into tomorrow, we should be running at full capacity,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told CBS News, while acknowledging continued delays.

But the situation has led to scrutiny over whether the nationwide ground-stop could have been prevented.

While President Donald Trump has blamed a lack of funding from Congress, critics say billions of dollars have already been allocated for badly needed upgrades. The work, they say, is what has lagged behind.

Democratic lawmakers have also questioned the Trump administration’s choice of contractors to install the upgrades.

“Secretary Duffy and the Federal Aviation Administration have received historical and monumental investments over the last two years,” Democratic Representative Rosa DeLauro said in a statement on Sunday.

“Congress has shown its willingness to modernize the FAA’s systems and support its workforce as part of annual bipartisan legislation, but we need a competent partner at the Department of Transportation to carry this out in a sustainable, transparent manner.”

Duffy has indicated that investigations are ongoing into what caused the malfunction on Friday.

But he has described the problem as starting at “a remote FAA location” where workers from the defence contractor L3Harris were replacing ageing copper wire with fibre optic lines.

A router used for communication reportedly began to malfunction, sending out 1,000 attempts to log onto the FAA’s system every four or five seconds, overloading the entire network.

In an interview on Sunday with NBC’s Meet the Press, Duffy stopped short of blaming L3Harris.

“Was this a faulty installation by L3Harris that was doing the work for us? Was it a fault of the router itself? We have to do that investigation and make sure we take precautions,” he said.

Though Duffy did suggest he preferred to part ways with the company, which owns a significant chunk of the FAA’s telecommunications infrastructure.

“I want to get away from L3Harris and get to a new one, but they own the network,” Duffy told Meet the Press. “I can’t cancel the network that they own, and I operate on.”

L3Harris has existed since 2019, following a merger between the Harris Corporation and L3 Technologies.

It is one of the largest defence contractors in the country, and its involvement with the FAA’s telecommunications network stretches back to 2002, when the Harris Corporation was awarded a billion-dollar contract to modernise the network’s systems.

But Friday’s mass grounding was not the first time L3Harris’s systems were involved in flight delays and problems with communications during an upgrade operation.

In November 2009, for example, the FAA’s network experienced a smaller outage as upgrades were being made to a router in Los Angeles, according to an agency investigation.

“The most notable impact to the flying public was the inability of the FAA to process electronic flight plan data,” a report explained.

“As a result, these flight plans had to be entered into the FAA air traffic control systems manually, causing the delay of over 800 flights that morning.”

In a statement after Friday’s grounding, L3Harris said it was supporting the FAA’s current probe and had already replaced 70 percent of the system’s copper wire with fibre optics.

“L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously,” it said.

Critics point out that many of the problems associated with the FAA’s telecommunications systems predate L3Harris’s involvement and stem from ageing infrastructure.

The FAA has aimed for years to replace some 5,170 lengths of copper wiring dating to the 1960s, which is used by routers and other communication gear.

Ageing copper, however, is just one of the tech problems the FAA faces.

In a September report, the Government Accountability Office, an independent agency tasked with reviewing government departments, highlighted a series of areas in dire need of upgrades.

Computers used by air traffic controllers to display key information like flight approach paths and aviation warnings were using obsolete hardware, including screens from the 1980s and floppy disk drives.

Thousands of radios and specialised switches that allow radio communication over phone lines also rely on obsolete technology that is no longer manufactured.

The agency had been forced to look for replacement parts on the online marketplace eBay, according to Duffy.

The Government Accountability Office also pointed to the continued use of paper flight strips, slips of paper printed for each flight coming into an air traffic controller’s area of responsibility.

Those documents help decide how to coordinate movements like takeoffs and landings so planes do not collide. But the print-out system has already caused dangerous situations.

In August 2023, for instance, a printer used to print flight strips at San Diego International airport jammed. As air traffic controllers tried to fix it, a Southwest Airlines aircraft almost hit a Cessna jet by about 30 metres (100 feet).

Before Friday’s incident, the last national ground stop happened in January 2023, after the FAA’s Notice to Airmen (NOTAM) system stopped working.

Built in 1985, the NOTAM system was responsible for sending emergency messages out about dangerous weather, congestion or other safety issues.

Its failure prompted the FAA to undertake a major review. The Government Accountability Office ultimately found that, out of the 138 systems the FAA relied on, 51 were unsustainable, and another 54 were potentially unsustainable because of ageing technology.

Fifty-eight of those systems, according to the accountability office, had a critical impact on the safety of air traffic in the US.

In September, the Government Accountability Office reported that the FAA had failed to meet at least four of its 11 recommendations for modernising air traffic systems.

One reason for the failure was the complexity of the upgrades. The FAA reportedly has 11,389 individual upgrade projects on its agenda, and it has struggled to coordinate the repairs, leaving it unable to prepare for network-wide problems.

The accountability office also determined that the FAA failed to make upgrades because it was not properly overseeing work done by its contractors.

It also pointed to a lack of funding. Unlike many critical government agencies, the FAA’s budget is not mandated by law, so Congress has to approve spending for the agency each year.

Even if Congress does allocate funding, the Trump administration does not have to use all of the money right away, and Democrats have pointed to unspent funds as part of the problem.

Though Congress allocated $12.5bn for the FAA’s upgrades in 2025, the Trump administration has only committed to spending $4bn of that sum. Only approximately $1bn has been spent so far.

Still, Duffy has argued that the FAA needs at least $50bn in the wake of Friday’s grounding.

Democrats like DeLauro have called that sum a “ransom without a real plan to deliver”. She urged full transparency from Duffy and the FAA.

“No federal leader should be free to do their work without Congressional oversight,” she said.

title: Czechs rally against gov’t threat to media independence

Czechs rally against gov’t threat to media independence

Tens of thousands rallied in Prague against the Czech government’s plan to scrap public media licence fees and shift funding to the state budget. Critics warn the move could undermine editorial independence and make public broadcasters more vulnerable to government influence.

title: Coles investigating ‘cybersecurity incident’ and apologises to customers
excerpt:
Supermarket giant says no customer, team or supplier data breached in cyber-attack but recommends customers update passwords

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australia’s s...
body_text:
Supermarket giant says no customer, team or supplier data breached in cyber-attack but recommends customers update passwords

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

Australia’s second-largest retailer has been targeted in a cyber-attack, though it is still too early to tell whether any of its data has been stolen or compromised.

Coles revealed the threat on Monday morning, saying it was investigating the incident with support from the Australian Cyber Security Centre and global security experts.

“Coles Group Limited is currently investigating a cyber security incident,” the company said in a statement to the stock exchange.

“We have not identified any evidence that customer, team or supplier data has been compromised or removed from Coles’ systems.

“Operations continue and customers are able to shop as normal with Coles in stores and online.”

Coles apologised to its customers for any concerns they might have at “a time of increasing cyber incidents in Australia and around the world”.

“We have security measures in place to protect customer and supplier accounts and are continuing to closely monitor our system,” it said.

“We recommend you regularly update your password with a strong, unique password for your account and not reuse the same password across multiple services.”

Coles also warned customers to be cautious if they receive unexpected emails or SMS messages purporting to be from the retailer, and not to click any links.

title: Blinken warns US ground invasion of Iran would be 'absolute disaster' as Tehran escalates attacks
excerpt:
Ret. Brig. Gen. John Teichert discusses Iran’s military capabilities following a drone attack aimed at Bahrain on ‘America Reports.’

Former Secretary of State Antony Blinken warned Saturday that airs...
body_text:
Ret. Brig. Gen. John Teichert discusses Iran’s military capabilities following a drone attack aimed at Bahrain on ‘America Reports.’

Former Secretary of State Antony Blinken warned Saturday that airstrikes alone may not eliminate Iran's weapons capabilities, but said a U.S. ground invasion would be an "absolute disaster."

Speaking at the 24th Hindustan Times Leadership Summit in New Delhi, Blinken, who served under President Biden, pointed to Iran's massive territory, population of roughly 90 million and ability to produce weapons deep inside the country as obstacles to any military campaign aimed at dismantling its arsenal.

"The weapons that it continues to produce are back far enough, the range is great enough that you can't just take everything out," Blinken said. "You'd probably have to have a land invasion of some kind to do that, which would be an absolute disaster."

TRUMP KEEPS SIGNALING AN END TO IRAN WAR, BUT EXPERT WARNS A CRUCIAL PIECE OF HIS STRATEGY IS MISSING

Former Secretary of State Antony Blinken said President Donald Trump's 20-point ceasefire agreement was based on the one developed by the Biden administration. (ARMEND NIMANI/AFP via Getty Images)

Blinken's warning came ahead of Iran claiming Sunday to have launched six drones at a U.S. military installation in Bahrain, while reports surfaced that neighboring Iraq faced concerns that its territory could be drawn into a potential American ground operation.

Bahrain said its air defenses blocked several Iranian aerial attacks Sunday, the first such interceptions since September.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it targeted a U.S. air defense radar system at the Al-Rifaa helicopter base with six drones in retaliation for what it described as "hostile US actions," according to Iranian state media, Reuters reported.

Bahraini officials said the drones were intercepted before reaching their targets.

IRAN HAS 'SUBSTANTIALLY INCREASED' EFFORTS TO TARGET AMERICANS ABROAD, US INTELLIGENCE MEMO WARNS

The locations of U.S. bases throughout the Gulf are seen in relation to Iran. (Fox News)

The latest escalation came amid further fighting in Yemen, where the Houthis made advances against Saudi-backed forces, raising additional concerns about the conflict spreading across the region.

Blinken warned that Iran retains the ability to widen the confrontation despite the United States' overwhelming conventional military superiority.

While Washington can "escalate vertically" by intensifying its bombing campaign, Blinken said, Tehran can "escalate horizontally" by targeting American military installations, regional allies and critical infrastructure, either directly or through allied armed groups.

"Even though we're much more powerful, that asymmetry in their ability to escalate horizontally as opposed to vertically is not to our advantage," Blinken said.

The former top diplomat also emphasized the geographic challenges facing U.S. forces.

"That coastline along the Strait of Hormuz goes on forever," Blinken said.

Iran is roughly four times the size of California, with a coastline and weapons production facilities that could complicate efforts to eliminate its military capabilities through air power alone.

TRUMP'S MOAB THREAT COULD PUT IRAN'S DEEPEST BUNKERS IN AMERICA'S CROSSHAIRS

Soldiers from the US-led coalition forces are seen during the handover of the K1 Air Base to the Iraqi Army from the US-led coalition in Kirkuk, Iraq on March 29, 2020. (Soldiers from the US-led coalition forces are seen during the handover of the K1 Air Base to the Iraqi Army from the US-led coalition in Kirkuk, Iraq on March 29, 2020)

Concerns about a potential ground operation have also intensified in neighboring Iraq, where officials have resisted proposals to sharply restrict trade and movement across the Iranian border.

Iran International reported that Tehran has become concerned that Iraqi territory could be used as a staging ground for a potential U.S. operation into southern Iran.

The Iraqi newspaper Al-Mada reported Nov. 9 that Iraq's prime minister privately briefed Shiite political leaders on an alleged American military plan involving a ground offensive, the outlet said.

In an interview with France 24 published Friday, Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein had also warned that the region's unstable security environment could not continue indefinitely.

The current state of "no war and no peace" is unsustainable, Hussein said, warning that the confrontation "either goes towards peace or it goes towards war."

AFTER 47 YEARS OF CONFRONTING IRAN, DOES AMERICA HAVE A STRATEGY FOR ENDING THIS WAR?

An MH-60R Sea Hawk helicopter lands on the flight deck of USS Rafael Peralta as it transits regional waters, in this photo released by U.S. Central Command on Oct. 15, 2026. CENTCOM said the USS Rafael Peralta is enforcing a military blockade of Iranian ports. (CENTCOM)

Hussein also said Baghdad has a responsibility to pursue diplomatic mediation because Iraq has already been drawn into the conflict.

He pointed to recent outreach to Tehran, including discussions with Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf.

The Iraqi foreign minister also rejected a reported U.S. demand that Baghdad close all but two of its land border crossings with Iran, describing the proposed restrictions as "not possible" and "a kind of sanction against the Iraqi people."

The border dispute comes as U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) expands efforts to disrupt Iranian weapons shipments and illicit trade through Task Force Iron Gate.

CENTCOM announced the task force would coordinate with other U.S. agencies to prevent Iran from transporting advanced weapons systems, dual-use technologies, sanctioned materials and illicit revenue across its land borders and the Caspian Sea.

Iraq shares a roughly 1,000-mile border with Iran.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: TikToker arrested after big cat mauls teen to death during video shoot at private farm
excerpt:
*Graphic Warning* A tiger fatally mauled a 19-year-old employee at a private breeding farm in Pakistan, where a TikToker had arrived to film a video, according to police and local reports.

A TikToker...
body_text:
*Graphic Warning* A tiger fatally mauled a 19-year-old employee at a private breeding farm in Pakistan, where a TikToker had arrived to film a video, according to police and local reports.

A TikToker has been arrested alongside a farm owner after a big cat viciously mauled a teenage employee to death during a video shoot in eastern Pakistan, officials said Thursday.

The attack happened at a private breeding farm near Kahna, according to The Times of India.

The animal "got out of control in the presence of the TikToker, who had come to the farmhouse to make a TikTok video, leaving a farm employee critically injured," Lahore police said in a post on X.

Although police described the animal as a lioness, a photo shared by the agency alongside its statement appeared to show a tiger.

'LOOKSMAXXING' INFLUENCER CLAVICULAR CHARGED AFTER ALLEGEDLY SHOOTING DEAD ALLIGATOR ON LIVESTREAM

A tiger reportedly released from its enclosure for a TikTok video fatally mauled a 19-year-old employee at a private breeding farm in Pakistan. (Lahore Police)

The victim, 19, was identified as Talha, while the arrested farm owner was identified as Fayyaz and the TikToker as Noman, according to The Times of India.

The outlet added that the TikToker had reportedly asked for the animal to be released from its enclosure for a TikTok video shoot.

After the attack, Talha was rushed to a private hospital but died while undergoing treatment.

Police arrested a TikToker and a farm owner after a teenage employee’s fatal mauling. (Lahore Police)

NEARLY 100 MONKEYS ESCAPE ENCLOSURE, INVADE NEIGHBORHOODS AS OFFICIALS SCRAMBLE TO RECAPTURE THEM

Police opened a case into the incident and uncovered an alleged attempt to "conceal the truth."

"An attempt was made to pass off the lioness attack as a dog attack," police said.

Investigators are examining whether the farm had the proper permits to keep the big cat, whether adequate safety measures were in place and whether negligence played a role in the attack.

Talha, 19, was rushed to a hospital after the attack but died while undergoing treatment. (Lahore Police)

The animal involved has also been handed over to wildlife authorities.

Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

title: Russia's mega-rich are already imagining a future after Putin
excerpt:
Hours after launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, Vladimir Putin gathered Russia's richest men in the Kremlin's cavernous Yekaterininsky Hall.

More than three dozen of the...
body_text:
Hours after launching his full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, Vladimir Putin gathered Russia's richest men in the Kremlin's cavernous Yekaterininsky Hall.

More than three dozen of them sat huddled along a wall, wearing face masks because of the Covid pandemic. One Russian newspaper reporter described them as "pale and sleep-deprived". On entering, Putin sat down at the opposite side of the hall, creating a vast space between him and the businessmen. As usual, he was wearing no mask.

Using his typically coded language, he said he expected them to support the war.

"I would like to call on you to show understanding of what is going on," he said, "and work together with the government to find the tools which would support production, the economy, jobs."

In the Kremlin-published video of the meeting, none of the invited billionaires said a word.

That silence has become a feature of the Russian super-rich. Over the decades of Putin's rule, they have learnt that the price of piping up could be high. In 2003, oil magnate Mikhail Khodorkovsky, Russia's richest man at the time, who was funding a number of opposition groups, accused Putin of presiding over rampant corruption. He spent the next 10 years behind bars, convicted of tax evasion, fraud and embezzlement - a warning to other would-be critics. He denied the charges.

The silence of Russian businessmen at a Kremlin summit with Putin in 2022 perhaps demonstrated their fear of the president

And even if any of the tycoons objected to the war, they have tended to keep their thoughts to themselves.

But even in that silence, there are murmurings: some members of Russia's once-mighty business elite seem to be imagining a Russia after Putin. They are wondering if, once the president has left office or died, the country might look more like it did in the 1990s, when the oligarchs enjoyed the fruits of power - or even if a healthier politics may take root.

The journalist Arkady Ostrovsky, a prominent Kremlin-watcher at The Economist newspaper who recently spent hours interviewing one of Russia's richest men, says he feels that a "historic, political shift is happening" in terms of how the ultra-rich view the future of the country.

The collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991 gave birth to a new, powerful force on the domestic scene: people who took advantage of the end of communism and became extraordinarily rich, and then wanted to control politicians for their own benefit. They were dubbed "the oligarchs", from Ancient Greek for the "few who rule".  They had money, which back then meant power.

This era of the "wild 1990s" was when the so-called "new Russians" burst onto the scene. Huge state companies came up for grabs, and men with the right connections became millionaires - even billionaires - almost overnight. Corruption was rife, cronyism rampant, and contract killings frequent.

But almost immediately after Putin was first elected as president in 2000, he subjugated the oligarchs. He had little interest in sharing power with anyone else. He could afford to stand up to the billionaires because Russia's economy was getting back on its feet, and the central government was getting stronger.

Some oligarchs developed a distinctive dress sense in the 1990s, as later satirised by this St Petersburg artist

Bill Browder, a financier who used to be the biggest foreign investor in Russia, and was banned from the country in 2005 after campaigning against corruption, says the Russian tycoons cowered and wilted in front of Putin - for example at the Davos economic forum, in the pre-war years when they were still welcomed there.

"I can remember seeing oligarchs walking around like they own the place, the most arrogant and self-confident individuals. And then Putin showed up, and it was just remarkable to see how these supposedly alpha-male-on-steroids individuals turned into absolutely subordinate, almost desperate schoolchildren," he tells the BBC.

Since the outbreak of war in 2022, the Kremlin has kept Russia's rich businessmen in line with a ruthless policy of carrot and stick. Critics of the war have seen their assets seized, while loyalists have been rewarded with lavish government war contracts: today there are more Russian billionaires than ever (155 in total, according to Forbes magazine).  Their collective wealth has reached a new high of nearly $700bn (£525bn).

But even for those tycoons who have stayed loyal and been rewarded, all of that money doesn't seem to be making them happy. Some are growing restless.

Their billions do not go as far as they used to: domestically, they cannot buy much political influence.

"They have no cards, they have no game," exiled politician and analyst Dmitry Nekrasov says. "They're rich because they've got something to do with Putin, not the other way round."

And outside of Russia, they are ostracised because of the Western sanctions imposed on Russia after its full-scale invasion.

"They're treated like low-level criminals. They can't fly their private jets. Their yachts can't park in all the best harbours in Europe. It must be very awful and humiliating for them," says Browder, the avowed Putin critic.

And so, quietly, some of their minds are turning to what happens after Putin leaves the scene. That's what I'm told by well-placed analysts, who are immersed in the world of these tycoons.

There's no immediate prospect of the president's departure, and there's no reason to think he's in bad health. But Putin, who turned 74 last month, has served in the Kremlin for a quarter of a century; people in Moscow know that his exit will come one day. When asked by Reuters last year if he intends to serve until 2036, when his constitutional term technically ends, Putin replied: "Only God knows if we have enough health."

One prominent oligarch of the 1990s was Boris Berezovsky, who fell out with the Kremlin and lived his later years in the UK

If Putin resigned or died in office, the prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, would take over. But Mishustin has not exhibited any presidential ambitions (that's probably a key reason he was appointed). That would create something of a power vacuum.

In that scenario, Russia-watchers I have spoken with envisage a few potential scenarios.

Some in the West, and no doubt within Russia, hope that democracy might flourish in a post-Putin Russia, with government led by the people, rather than by a new cadre of oligarchs or a single autocrat. But this seems like the least likely path, analysts say. Key democratic institutions have been eroded or destroyed over Putin's rule. "Russia is so used to violence, it has grown unaccustomed to standard democratic procedures," says Alexandra Prokopenko, an exiled Russian journalist and analyst.

Another path is more autocracy. A different figure could replace Putin and continue his culture of repression. But Prokopenko thinks this wouldn't be another strongman dictatorship - at least not right away. These things take time, she says: at first, Putin's successor would be weaker than him, with fewer resources.

And then there's the third option: tycoons re-assert their power and Russia returns to something resembling a 1990s-style system of oligarchy. Dmitry Nekrasov, a former Kremlin adviser and opposition politician who now lives in exile, says under this scenario, the country would be governed by a handful of powerful elite clans in alliance with business interests.

This last option, of course, is the one that many tycoons want. "They'd like to return to a time when they were listened to, when they were not stripped of assets and when they understood the rules of the game," says Prokopenko, who has spent a lot of time speaking to Russia's richest people.

Though their power has been seriously curtailed since the 1990s, it's still worth listening to the tycoons: given their immense wealth, it seems likely that sooner or later they will try to re-assert their political influence.

Already, some are "trying to be friends with the right sort of security officials or ministers", says Nekrasov, the exiled politician. But he says any further steps are "too dangerous to take".

Putin has kept tycoons in line with a ruthless policy of carrot and stick since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine

He says the behaviour of the tycoons in coming years will depend in part on their finances. Those who have lots of liquid cash will be more confident to "play political games" and jockey for position, preparing for a post-Putin country. But those whose wealth is dependent on state contracts or government goodwill will feel too afraid, in case they lose everything, he says.

Prokopenko says there's already been a shift in how the businessmen talk about Putin. They used to nickname him "Nachalnik" (which translates as "boss"), as well as "Perviy" ("first"), or by his initials "VV" - all nicknames that convey a degree of respect. Now they call him "Ded", with what Prokopenko calls "a pinch of contempt". "Ded" translates as "oldie" or "granddad" - a much less reverent name.

Some rich Russians are pining after a "return of politics into people's lives", she says, with less repression, more open speech, and healthier competition between parties and politicians.

But at the moment, she says, they are too afraid to make that happen due to Russia's stifling atmosphere. Prokopenko interviewed one tycoon who physically sat on his phone during the whole conversation, because he thought it would make digital eavesdropping more difficult for secret police. "I thought that it's an absolutely Stalinistic type of fear. It's absolutely irrational," she says.

An interesting clue for what tycoons might want from a post-Putin future came from Andrey Melnichenko, who is known as the world's fertiliser king and is currently Russia's eighth richest man.

Earlier this year, he surprised observers by giving an interview to The Economist - a rare thing for a rich Russian to do, especially to a publication from a country the Kremlin considers unfriendly. They also published an essay written by him.

In parts of the interview, Melnichenko repeated Kremlin talking points. He said that Ukraine is a battlefield between Russia and the West, and he thinks the West ignored Russia's security concerns and threatens its sovereignty.

But then it got more interesting. Melnichenko did not call for Putin to go, but - and it's a big but - he argued for a change that would bring about an end to one-man rule in Russia. He said Russia needs to engage more with the world.

Prokopenko thinks the tycoon was trying to stir a public conversation. It was a "call on rich people like him to start talking", she says.

The journalist who interviewed him, Arkady Ostrovsky, tells me the pair had "tense and heated discussions" in "hotels and cafes, mostly drinking coffee, lots of coffee, sometimes smoking". He says the tycoon seemed to be "genuinely thinking" about his answers, rather than giving politician-style spin.

Nothing in Russia is simple, and most observers think the interview probably happened with some form of approval - implicit or explicit - from the Kremlin. We don't know why authorities would have been happy to authorise the unusual call for change; it's possible they were trying to show that some degree of pluralism still exists in the country.

No tycoons came out to support him. Still, the journalist feels that Melnichenko was not speaking for himself alone, but also for his fellow businessmen.

Some tycoons feel ostracised because of Western sanctions, unable to fly private jets and visit Western resorts like Saint-Jean-Cap-Ferrat in southern France, which used to be popular with rich Russians

Some of them are hoping that after Putin's departure, the country might become an "oligarchic republic", as journalist Ostrovsky puts it - something like how it looked in the 1990s, with the business elites in charge.

Based on his years of reporting on Russia, Ostrovsky says that many of the country's mega-rich currently feel a "sense of complete dead end, which this war has led Russia to… [an] absence of the future".

But even if the tycoons are thinking about the future, there's a slim prospect of them acting any time soon, it seems.

Browder, the Putin critic, says that although many of them are unhappy, they're unlikely to conspire against Putin while he is still alive. "They understand that if they were to do anything that would challenge Putin, he would kill them. And Putin is a very paranoid little man."

Mike Calvey, an American financier who used to be a key investor in Russia, agrees. "What can they do besides just go straight to the prison and lose their assets? It's easy for people who are sitting in London to say that, 'why don't you just all go stand up and go straight to prison?' That's really what would happen."

Russia's richest men used to be able to pull strings at the highest levels of power. Once Putin is gone, there is no doubt they will try to claw back their past influence. The question is: will remnants of the current regime let them?

Spain and China are cosying up - to the anger of many in the EU

Europe's youth is on the march - but does anything actually unite them?
